Logit Distance Bounds Representational Similarity

Beatrix M. G. Nielsen ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: IT University of Copenhagen Email: beat@itu.dk    Emanuele Marconato11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Trento Email: emanuele.marconato@unitn.it    Luigi Gresele ††thanks: Shared last author. Affiliation: University of Copenhagen Email: lg@math.ku.dk    Andrea Dittadi22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Helmholtz Munich & TUM Email: andrea.dittadi@gmail.com    Simon Buchholz22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: MPI IS, Tübingen Email: sbuchholz@tue.mpg.de
Abstract

For a broad family of discriminative models that includes autoregressive language models, identifiability results imply that if two models induce the same conditional distributions, then their internal representations agree up to an invertible linear transformation. We ask whether an analogous conclusion holds approximately when the distributions are close instead of equal. Building on the observation of Nielsen et al. (2025) that closeness in KL divergence need not imply high linear representational similarity, we study a distributional distance based on logit differences and show that closeness in this distance does yield linear similarity guarantees. Specifically, we define a representational dissimilarity measure based on the models’ identifiability class and prove that it is bounded by the logit distance. We further show that, when model probabilities are bounded away from zero, KL divergence upper-bounds logit distance; yet the resulting bound fails to provide nontrivial control in practice. As a consequence, KL-based distillation can match a teacher’s predictions while failing to preserve linear representational properties, such as linear-probe recoverability of human-interpretable concepts. In distillation experiments on synthetic and image datasets, logit-distance distillation yields students with higher linear representational similarity and better preservation of the teacher’s linearly recoverable concepts.

1 Introduction

It is widely believed that the success of deep learning models depends on the data representation they learn Bengio et al. (2013); yet it is unclear what properties “good” representations have in common Bansal et al. (2021). Accordingly, prior work studies when models with comparable performance exhibit similar internal representations Morcos et al. (2018); Kornblith et al. (2019); Klabunde et al. (2025) and how human-interpretable concepts are encoded within them Bricken et al. (2023); Gurnee and Tegmark (2023). Empirically, many such concepts can be predicted from internal representations by simple linear probes Alain and Bengio (2016); Kim et al. (2018), suggesting substantial linear structure in the representations of successful models Mikolov et al. (2013); Park et al. (2024). However, this regularity is not universal Engels et al. (2024); Li et al. (2025a), and it remains unclear to what extent linear representational properties are consistently shared across models that perform comparably well on the same task.

We study this question for a broad family of discriminative models, including autoregressive next-token prediction. Prior identifiability results show that, under a suitable diversity assumption, if two such models induce the same conditional distribution, then their representations are equal up to an invertible linear transformation Khemakhem et al. (2020b); Roeder et al. (2021); Lachapelle et al. (2023), and one can characterize which linear properties are shared across the equivalence class (Marconato et al., 2025). A key question is whether these conclusions hold approximately when two models induce distributions that are close but not equal (Buchholz and Schölkopf, 2024). Nielsen et al. (2025) show that the answer depends on how distributional closeness is measured: in particular, models can be arbitrarily close in KL divergence while their representations remain far from linearly related. On the other hand, robustness can be recovered under suitable divergences for which distributional closeness does imply representational similarity.

In this work, we ask: when two models in this family induce similar conditional distributions, to what extent do their representations agree up to an invertible linear map? We introduce a distributional distance based on logit differences and prove quantitative representation-level guarantees: small logit distance (i) implies high linear representational similarity, yielding an explicit lower bound on mCCA between representation spaces Raghu et al. (2017); Morcos et al. (2018) and (ii) upper-bounds a representational dissimilarity measure that we design to respect the model family’s equivalence class. Finally, we clarify the (limited) extent to which KL control can recover such guarantees: if model probabilities are bounded away from zero, then the KL divergence upper-bounds the logit distance, but the resulting tight robustness bounds are insufficient for practical settings.

Our results have an immediate implication for knowledge distillation. Standard approaches train a student to match a teacher’s predictions by minimizing a KL divergence between output distributions Hinton et al. (2015); yet our theory implies that a student can be very close to its teacher in KL while still learning representations far from being linearly aligned. This motivates alternative objectives, and our theory suggests that minimizing logit differences—an approach considered in prior distillation work (Ba and Caruana, 2014; Menon et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021)— should yield representations that are closer to being linearly equivalent. Empirically, we compare vanilla (KL-based) distillation to logit-distance distillation and find that the latter preserves the teacher’s representational structure substantially better, both in terms of representational similarity measured by mCCA and our metric (on a synthetic dataset and CIFAR 100100 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009)) and in terms of downstream linear properties recoverable by probing (on the SUB dataset (Bader et al., 2025)). Overall, our work clarifies when linear properties are approximately shared across models whose distributions are close, and suggests a practical distillation takeaway: if representational similarity matters, KL is the wrong loss; a logit-distance objective is a better one.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We analyze a logit-difference distance between conditional distributions and show it is a proper metric for the model family we consider (Section 3).

  • •

    We show KL divergence can upper-bound logit distance under strong assumptions (Section 3.1), but the resulting bounds do not yield meaningful representation guarantees in typical regimes.

  • •

    We propose a representation dissimilarity measure which is zero if and only if models are in the same linear equivalence class (Section 3.3).

  • •

    We prove that small logit distance implies high linear representational similarity, giving quantitative guarantees both for mCCA (Section 3.2), our dissimilarity measure (Section 3.4) and for linearly encoded concepts (Section 4).

  • •

    In distillation experiments, we show empirically that logit matching preserves the teacher’s representational structure better than KL-based distillation (Section 5).

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the notation and model family, recall its linear identifiability under a diversity assumption, and formulate the question of approximate identifiability that motivates our analysis.

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} denote the input space, either continuous or discrete. We assume a data distribution p𝐱p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} supported on supp⁡(p𝐱)⊆𝒳\mathrm{supp}(p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\subseteq\mathcal{X}, and a finite label set 𝒴\mathcal{Y} of size kk, such as tokens in a language model or class labels in a classification problem. We focus on a broad model family which encompasses autoregressive language models (Radford et al., 2019), methods for self-supervised pretraining for image classification (Oord et al., 2018), and several supervised classifiers (Khemakhem et al., 2020b; Ibrahim et al., 2024). We denote this model family by Θ\Theta. Each element (𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta induces a conditional distribution p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}), where 𝐟:𝒳→ℝm{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} is the embedding function and 𝐠:𝒴→ℝm{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} the unembedding function. The conditional distribution takes the form

(1)

∑y∈𝒴𝐠⁡(y)=𝟎⟹∑i=1ku​(𝐱)i=0.\textstyle\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)=\mathbf{0}\implies\sum_{i=1}^{k}u({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{i}=0\,. (3)

Identifiability of the model class. Several works (Khemakhem et al., 2020b; Roeder et al., 2021; Lachapelle et al., 2023; Marconato et al., 2025; Reizinger et al., 2025; Nielsen et al., 2025) have investigated the symmetries belonging to the model class for which, two different choices of embeddings and unembeddings, say (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta, generate the same conditional probability distribution. In our setting, similar to (Nielsen et al., 2025), we study the case where labels are abundant and their number exceeds that of the representations, i.e., k>mk>m. Below, we report the linear identifiability result from (Roeder et al., 2021). This requires an extra condition, known as diversity, which can be interpreted as a restriction to models that span the whole representation space (Marconato et al., 2025).

Assumption 2.1 (Diversity).

A model (𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta satisfies the diversity condition if

dim⁡(span⁡{𝐮⁡(𝐱):𝐱∈supp⁡(p𝐱)})=m.\mathrm{dim}\big(\mathrm{span}\{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}):{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathrm{supp}(p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\}\big)=m\,. (5)

In particular, there exists a choice of y~∈𝒴\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y} and 𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}, for which 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} (Eq. 4) is invertible.

This condition gives the following result.

Theorem 2.2 (Linear Identifiability).

For two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta that satisfy the diversity condition (Assumption 2.1), let y~∈𝒴\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y} and 𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\} be a choice of pivot point and mm labels such that 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} is invertible. Let 𝐀~𝒥≔𝐋~𝒥−⁣⊤​𝐋~𝒥′⁣⊤∈ℝm×m{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\coloneqq\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}}. Let ∼L\sim_{L} be the equivalence relation in Θ\Theta, such that (𝐟,𝐠)∼L(𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\sim_{L}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) if and only if there exists a matrix 𝐀{\bm{\mathrm{A}}} such that

𝐟⁡(𝐱)=𝐀𝐟′​(𝐱),𝐠~​(y)=𝐀−⁣⊤​𝐠~′​(y).\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})={\bm{\mathrm{A}}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),\quad\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)={\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{-\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y)\,. (6)

Then we have that

p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)=p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱),∀(𝐱,y)∈𝒳×𝒴⇔(𝐟,𝐠)∼L(𝐟′,𝐠′).\displaystyle\begin{split}&p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),\;\forall({\bm{\mathrm{x}}},y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\\ &\iff({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\sim_{L}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\,.\end{split} (7)

In particular, we can set 𝐀=𝐀~𝒥{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}=\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}.

This result shows that when the distributions generated by two models are equal and satisfy the diversity condition, their representations are related by an invertible linear transformation given by 𝐀~𝒥∈ℝm×m\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}. We show in Proposition C.1 that the form of 𝐀~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}} does not depend on the choice of y~\tilde{y} and 𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\} as long as the matrix 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} is invertible.

Closeness in distribution and representational similarity. The result in Theorem 2.2 assumes exact equality of conditional distributions. In practice, however, independently trained models will almost never satisfy this condition exactly, even when trained on the same data. This raises the question of whether the identifiability conclusion is robust: namely, whether models whose distributions are merely close, rather than equal, must also have similar internal representations up to the model class’s intrinsic symmetry (an invertible linear change of basis).

This question was first systematically investigated by Nielsen et al. (2025). Addressing it requires specifying (i) a notion of distance between conditional distributions and (ii) a notion of dissimilarity between representations. For the latter, we require the dissimilarity to vanish for ∼L\sim_{L}-linearly equivalent models. This is because, for any p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}), different reparametrizations of (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) exists that do not change the probability distribution (by Theorem 2.2). With this requirement in place, our goal is to identify distributional distances for which small discrepancies in conditional distributions provably imply small representational dissimilarity.

3 The Logit Distance and Connection to Representational Similarity

We now define a metric between distributions from our model family.

Definition 3.1.

Let p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′′p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}^{\prime} be two sets of conditional distributions arising from two models from our model class. We denote by dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} the following logit distance

dlogit2​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′′)=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖22.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2}^{2}\;. (8)

Notice that dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} coincides with the square root of the mean squared error between models’ logits. This can be written in terms of log-probabilities (see Appendix D.1 for details), and the expression ∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert_{2} corresponds to the Aitchison distance (see Section D.2) of the conditional distributions p𝐟,𝐠(⋅|𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) and p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) which is a metric in compositional data analysis (Aitchison et al., 2000; Pawlowsky-Glahn et al., 2007). We show in Section D.3 that Definition 3.1 is a metric (potentially with infinite value) between distributions from models in our model class. A sufficient condition for dlogit​(p,p′)<∞d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime})<\infty, is that the probabilities are lower bounded by some τ>0\tau>0 for all y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} and 𝐱∈𝒳{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathcal{X}.

3.1 KL Divergence Bounds Logit Distance

We consider the relationship between the logit distance and the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence which both measure the closeness between two distributions. Following Nielsen et al. (2025), given (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta, we consider

dKL(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟,𝐠′)≔𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱[KL(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱)||p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅∣𝐱))],d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}[\mathrm{KL}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))]\,, (9)

which is related to the cross-entropy loss

ℒp​(𝐟′,𝐠′)=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱,y∼p⁡(y∣𝐱)​[−log⁡p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y|𝐱)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{p}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}},y\sim p(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}[-\log p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})] (10)

for a well-specified model through

dKL​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟,𝐠′)=ℒp𝐟,𝐠​(𝐟′,𝐠′)−ℒp𝐟,𝐠​(𝐟,𝐠).\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})=\mathcal{L}_{p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})-\mathcal{L}_{p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}}({{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}},{{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}})\;. (11)

This means that learning a model (𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta on data sampled from a distribution p𝐟,𝐠p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}} in the model class, will be equivalent in expectation to minimizing dKL​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}). However, Nielsen et al. (2025, Theorem 3.1) show that the equivalence relation ∼L\sim_{L} is not robust to small changes in the probability distribution as measured by dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}}. Specifically, they construct pairs (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) and (𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) with arbitrarily small KL divergence, yet whose representations cannot be made close by any invertible linear map (low mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}). This can happen because, without additional regularity assumptions on Θ\Theta, models may assign extremely small probabilities to some events. Changes concentrated on such near-zero-probability events can correspond to large (potentially nonlinear) changes in representation geometry while incurring only a negligible increase in dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}}. To rule out these corner cases, we restrict attention to models (𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta whose probability assignments are uniformly lower bounded by some constant τ>0\tau>0.

Assumption 3.2 (τ\tau-lower bounded).

For τ>0\tau>0, we say that a model (𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta is τ\tau-lower bounded if, for p𝐱p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}-almost every 𝐱∈𝒳{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathcal{X}, we have

miny∈𝒴⁡p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)≥τ.\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\geq\tau\,. (12)

We also show in Section E.1 that this is equivalent to having bounded embeddings and unembeddings. We can now prove the next result (full proof in Section E.2).

Theorem 3.3.

For two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta, we have

dlogit2​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′′)≥2​dKL​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′).d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}^{\prime})\geq 2d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})\,. (13)

If there exists 0<τ<1/30<\tau<1/3 such that both (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) and (𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) are τ\tau-lower bounded (Assumption 3.2), then

dlogit2​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′′)≤4​log⁡(τ)2τ​dKL​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′).d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}^{\prime})\leq\frac{4\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})\,. (14)

In contrast to the general setting discussed above—where arbitrarily small dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} may still correspond to highly dissimilar representations—Theorem 3.3 shows that, under the additional τ\tau-boundedness assumption, the KL divergence does bound the logit distance. As we show below, this in turn implies that dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} also bounds representation dissimilarity. However, the upper bound in (14) is only quantitatively meaningful when dKL=O⁡(τ)d_{\mathrm{KL}}=O(\tau), since the bound scales as τ−1\tau^{-1} up to logarithmic factors. As τ≤1/k\tau\leq 1/k in a kk-class setting and is typically much smaller in practice, this condition can be restrictive. We remark that a similar but weaker bound holds when only one of the models (e.g., a constrained student) is τ\tau-bounded (see Lemma E.4). Moreover, the dependence on τ\tau is tight up to logarithmic terms.

3.2 Logit Distance Bounds Mean CCA

We next show that the representations are approximately linearly related when the distance between the logits of two models is small. Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) (Hotelling, 1936) is a common way of measuring whether sets of vectors are linearly related (see Section B.1). We denote by mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}} the mean canonical correlation which is 1 when two vector-valued variables are almost surely linear transformations of each other. In our setting, the pair of variables will be either a pair of embeddings or unembeddings from two different models.

Theorem 3.4.

Let mm be the dimension of the representations. Let μm\mu_{m} be the mm-th eigenvalue of the matrix 𝚺𝐮,𝐮≔𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​[𝐮⁡(𝐱)​𝐮​(𝐱)⊤]−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​[𝐮⁡(𝐱)]​𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​[𝐮​(𝐱)⊤]{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}}\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\big[{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}\big]-\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\big[{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})]\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\big[{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}\big]. Assume μm>0\mu_{m}>0. Then we have

mCCA​(𝐟⁡(𝐱),𝐟′​(𝐱))≥1−dlogit2​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′′)m​μm\displaystyle m_{\mathrm{CCA}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))\geq 1-\frac{d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}^{\prime})}{m\mu_{m}} (15)

and the same bound holds for mCCA​(𝐠⁡(y),𝐠′​(y))m_{\mathrm{CCA}}({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y),{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y)).

Full proof in Section F.4. We emphasize that this result is invariant to linear transformations (𝐟,𝐠)↦(𝐀𝐟,𝐀−⁣⊤​𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\mapsto({\bm{\mathrm{A}}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{-\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}). The theorem shows that, with a small difference in distributions in terms of dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} of two models, we get similar representations in terms of mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}. In particular, if the distributions of p𝐟,𝐠p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}} and p𝐟′,𝐠′p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}} agree, we conclude that mCCA​(𝐟⁡(𝐱),𝐟′​(𝐱))=1m_{\mathrm{CCA}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))=1, which means that there exists a matrix 𝐁{\bm{\mathrm{B}}} such that 𝐟​(𝐱)=𝐁𝐟′​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})={\bm{\mathrm{B}}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) for all 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} and similarly 𝐠⁡(y)=𝐁~​𝐠​(y){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)=\tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y) for another matrix 𝐁~\tilde{\mathbf{B}}. Therefore this result generalizes the linear identifiability of 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} in Theorem 2.2 to models that are similar in terms of dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} or dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} (via Theorem 3.3). However, having mCCA​(𝐟⁡(𝐱),𝐟′​(𝐱))=1m_{\mathrm{CCA}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))=1 and small KL divergence is not sufficient to conclude that the joint representations (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) and (𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) are similar (see Appendix G for an example), and while we can conclude that 𝐁=𝐁~−⁣⊤{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}=\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{-\top} holds for dlogit=0d_{\mathrm{logit}}=0 and thus recover the identifiability result, no rates for the error can be obtained when dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} is positive (see Appendix F.3). This motivates the study of further dissimilarity measures which naturally incorporate the relation of embeddings and unembeddings and therefore better match the linear identifiability result.

3.3 Linear Identifiability Dissimilarity

In this section we define a dissimilarity measure, drepd_{\mathrm{rep}}, between representations inspired by Theorem 2.2, in the sense that it is zero if and only if the representations are linearly equivalent. We first notice that linear equivalence in Theorem 2.2, mediated by 𝐀~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, necessitates a choice of pivot point and mm other labels so that 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} is invertible. Since we do not want the invertibility to depend on the choice, we introduce the following assumption:

Assumption 3.5.

A model (𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta is in general position if, for every y~∈𝒴\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y} and 𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}, the matrix 𝐋~𝒥∈ℝm×m\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} (Eq. 4) is invertible, and the embeddings span the representation space: span⁡{𝐟⁡(𝐱):𝐱∈supp⁡(p𝐱)}=ℝm\mathrm{span}\{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}):{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathrm{supp}(p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\}=\mathbb{R}^{m}.

This assumption naturally requires that for any choice of pivot point, y~\tilde{y}, the shifted unembeddings 𝐠~​(y)\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y) are in general position (Cover, 1965).22 2 We say n≥mn\geq m vectors are in general position in ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m} if, for any choice of mm or fewer vectors, these are linearly independent. It also ensures that the diversity condition (Assumption 2.1) is satisfied. For models satisfying Assumption 3.5, Theorem 2.2 gives us the following corollary:

Corollary 3.6.

For two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta that satisfy Assumption 3.5. If p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)=p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱),∀(𝐱,y)∈𝒳×𝒴p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),\;\forall({\bm{\mathrm{x}}},y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} then for every choice of pivot point and mm labels, we have

𝐟⁡(𝐱)=𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱) and 𝐠~​(y)=𝐀~𝒥−⁣⊤​𝐠~′​(y).\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\quad\text{ and }\quad\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)=\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y)\,. (16)

Equivalently, if there exists a choice of pivot and labels such that the linear relation does not hold, then ∃𝐱,y\exists{\bm{\mathrm{x}}},y s.t. p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)≠p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\neq p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}).

Therefore, if we want to make a dissimilarity measure which measures how far the representations are from being in the same equivalence class —independent of the choice of pivot points and labels— we have to consider the error for all possible choices of labels which can be used to construct the 𝐀~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}} matrix. We capture this in the definition below.

Definition 3.7.

Let J=(k−1m)J=\binom{k-1}{m}. For any two choices of models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta satisfying Assumption 3.5, the squared linear identifiability dissimilarity is given by

drep2​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))≔1k​J​∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖22.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{rep}}^{2}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))\coloneq\frac{1}{kJ}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2}^{2}\;.

The linear identifiability dissimilarity in Definition 3.7 averages the squared distance between 𝐟⁡(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) and 𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) over every choice of pivot and labels and every input. We see that by Corollary 3.6, if the distributions of (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) and (𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) are equal, then drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} is zero. Next, we will show that using the logit distance between distributions, this can be bounded. We will also show that if drep​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))=0d_{\mathrm{rep}}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))=0 then distributions are also equal.

3.4 Logit Distance Bounds Representational Distance

In this section, we show that, for our model family, the logit distance is zero if and only if the linear identifiability dissimilarity vanishes and that the former bounds the latter. As a corollary, we show that this bound extends also to KL. Full proofs for this section are in Appendix H.

We note that, for two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta that satisfy Assumption 3.5, the squared logit distance can be written as a sum of terms of the form ‖𝐁−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖22\big\|{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}^{-\top}\big({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\big)\big\|_{2}^{2} for a matrix 𝐁{\bm{\mathrm{B}}} related to the SVD decomposition of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} (see Theorem H.1 for the precise statement). This shows that the logit difference is naturally connected to the linear identifiability dissimilarity and gives us the following corollary:

Corollary 3.8.

For (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta satisfying Assumption 3.5, we have

drep​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))=0⇔dlogit​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)=0.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{rep}}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))=0\iff d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})=0\,.

Moreover, we can upper (and lower, see Section H.2) bound drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} using dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} and the singular values of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}.

Theorem 3.9.

Let p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}} be as before, and mm the dimension of the representations. Let C=2​mk−1C=\sqrt{\frac{2m}{k-1}}. Let σmin\sigma_{\min} be the smallest singular value of all 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}. Then dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}}, bounds the linear identifiability dissimilarity drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} as follows:

drep​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))≤C​dlogit​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)σmin.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{rep}}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))\leq C\;\frac{d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})}{\sigma_{\min}}\;. (17)

Interestingly, this result highlights that the connection between distributional distance and representational dissimilarity is tightly connected to both embeddings and unembeddings. In fact, the bound depends on the minimum singular value among the unembeddings matrices 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, i.e., σmin\sigma_{\min}, accounting for the direction in embedding space of minimum variation of the shifted unembeddings. In particular, small values of dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} will ensure that the embeddings of the two models are close to being a linear invertible transformation of each other, where the transformation is mediated by the unembeddings. This also links to a bound on drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} through dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} when models have lower bounded probabilities:

Corollary 3.10.

Let (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta be two models from our model class (1) which satisfy Assumption 3.2 and Assumption 3.5 . Let C=2​mk−1C=\sqrt{\frac{2m}{k-1}} and CK​L=2​C​|log⁡(τ)|τC_{KL}=\frac{2C|\log(\tau)|}{\sqrt{\tau}}. Then

drep​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))≤CK​L​dKL​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)σmin.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{rep}}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))\leq C_{KL}\frac{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})}}{\sigma_{\min}}\,. (18)

4 Applications: Distillation and Interpretability

Knowledge distillation (KD) aims to train a compact student model to match the predictive distribution of a larger teacher. In its original formulation (Hinton et al., 2015), KD combines a supervised cross-entropy loss, ℒp𝒟\mathcal{L}_{p_{\mathcal{D}}}, on the data distribution p𝒟​(y∣𝐱)p_{\mathcal{D}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) with a KL divergence term that aligns the student distribution with that of a fixed teacher (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) with distribution p𝐟,𝐠p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}. The student (𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) with distribution p𝐟′​𝐠′p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}} is obtained by solving

(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈argmin(𝐟∗,𝐠∗)∈Θ(ℒp𝒟​(𝐟∗,𝐠∗)+dKL​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟∗,𝐠∗))({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\argmin_{({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{*},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{*})\in\Theta}\big(\mathcal{L}_{p_{\mathcal{D}}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{*},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{*})+d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{*},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{*}})\big)

typically using only a small subset of training samples. A large body of work explores refinements of this objective to better match the teacher distribution (Mansourian et al., 2025), including alternative formulations of the KL term (Zhao et al., 2022) or by considering an equivalent loss to dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} (Navaneet et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021). When available, the teacher’s intermediate activations can further guide training (Romero et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2023), with regression on embeddings or unembeddings encouraging closer representational alignment.

Our analysis highlights that, when only teacher probabilities are available, the original dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} minimization does not significantly bound representational similarity (as measured with drepd_{\mathrm{rep}}) between teacher and student. When only teacher probabilities or logits are available, a better learning target is to minimize an equivalent loss to dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}}. Apart from using dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} as a loss directly, we consider training with a L1L_{1} variant of the logit distance between teacher logits 𝐮{\bm{\mathrm{u}}} and student 𝐮′{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}, that is

ℒlogit1​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)≔𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖1,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{logit}}^{1}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})\coloneq\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{1}\,, (19)

Using ℒlogit1\mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathrm{logit}} improves training stability (Qi et al., 2020) and, importantly, still leads to decreasing dlogit​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}):

Proposition 4.1.

For two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta which both satisfy Assumption 3.2 for some τ>0\tau>0, then

dlogit2​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)≤2​|log⁡(τ)|​ℒlogit1​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′).\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})\leq 2|\log(\tau)|\mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathrm{logit}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})\,. (20)

In particular, with this result we have that minimizing ℒlogit1\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{logit}}^{1} will naturally reduce dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} between the teacher and student distributions, independently of the representation dimensionality of the two. Full proof in Appendix J.

Interpretable properties. Prior works have investigated whether model embeddings linearly encode latent, interpretable concepts (Mikolov et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2018; Engels et al., 2024). For example, Marks and Tegmark (2023) showed that the truth value of a statement 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} can be approximated by a linear function of its language model embedding 𝐟⁡(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}). Similar forms of linear separability have also been studied in pretrained neural networks for visual concepts in image classification (Alain and Bengio, 2016).

Formally, we define a categorical concept as a function 𝐡:𝒳→ΔC−1{\bm{\mathrm{h}}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta^{C-1}, where ΔC−1\Delta^{C-1} is the simplex over C≥2C\geq 2 values, giving a distribution over concept values

p𝐡​(c∣𝐱):=𝐡​(𝐱)c,∀c∈{1,…,C}.p_{\bm{\mathrm{h}}}(c\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}):={\bm{\mathrm{h}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{c},\;\forall c\in\{1,\ldots,C\}\,. (21)

Inspired by previous works (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Rajendran et al., 2024), we propose a definition that captures linear separability of concepts from model embeddings:

Definition 4.2 (Linearly encoded concept 𝐡{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} in 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}).

For a concept 𝐡:𝒳→ΔC−1{\bm{\mathrm{h}}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta^{C-1}, with C≥2C\geq 2, giving a distribution p𝐡p_{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} as in Eq. 21, we say that that 𝐡{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} is linearly encoded in 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} if there exist CC linear weights 𝐰c∈ℝm{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and biases bc∈ℝb_{c}\in\mathbb{R} such that, for all c∈{1,…,C}c\in\{1,\ldots,C\},

exp⁡(𝐰c⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)+bc)∑j=1Cexp⁡(𝐰j⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)+bj)=p𝐡​(c∣𝐱).\frac{\exp\big({\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{c}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})+b_{c}\big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{C}\exp\big({\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{j}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})+b_{j}\big)}=p_{\bm{\mathrm{h}}}(c\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\,. (22)

Then, we indicate with 𝐖∈ℝm×C{\bm{\mathrm{W}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times C} the matrix of weights 𝐰c{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{c} and with 𝐛∈ℝC{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} the vector of biases bcb_{c}.

In words, Definition 4.2 states that the probability assignments over concept values defined by p𝐡p_{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} can be recovered through a linear function of the model embeddings. This also implies that the embedding space is partitioned linearly into convex regions, each corresponding to the most likely concept label (Snell et al., 2017), as illustrated in Fig. 1 (left). Crucially, we show that dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} bounds the degree to which concepts are shared between models that are close:

Theorem 4.3.

For two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta and a concept 𝐡:𝒳→ΔC−1{\bm{\mathrm{h}}}:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta^{C-1} with C≥2C\geq 2, if 𝐡{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} is linearly encoded in 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}, then

min𝐖′,𝐛′⁡dKL​(p𝐡CLOSE\displaystyle\textstyle\min_{{\bm{\mathrm{W}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}^{\prime}}d_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(p_{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} ,softmax(𝐖′⊤𝐟′(⋅)+𝐛′))≤12∥𝐀∥o​p2dlogit2(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′),\displaystyle,\mathrm{softmax}\big({\bm{\mathrm{W}}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}(\cdot)+{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}^{\prime})\big)\leq\frac{1}{2}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}\rVert_{op}^{2}d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})\,, (23)

where ∥⋅∥op\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathrm{op}} denotes the operator norm, 𝐀{\bm{\mathrm{A}}} is determined by 𝐖=𝐋𝐀{\bm{\mathrm{W}}}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}, 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} is the unembedding matrix, and 𝐖{\bm{\mathrm{W}}}, 𝐛{\bm{\mathrm{b}}} are obtained from Definition 4.2.

This result (proof in Appendix I) also shows that equality between model distributions preserves linearly encoded concepts between models that are linearly equivalent, mirroring previous results (Park et al., 2023; Marconato et al., 2025).

5 Experiments

Datasets. We evaluate all methods on three datasets: (1) Synth is a synthetically generated dataset with two-dimensional inputs and 77 labels. The inputs are designed so that the labels are not linearly separable (see Fig. 2 for an illustration). We train models with (m=2)(m=2)-dimensional representations. (2) CIFAR 100100 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009) consists of natural images from 100100 classes. We use representations of dimension m=50m=50. (3) SUB (Bader et al., 2025) is a high-quality synthetic variant of CUB200 (Wah et al., 2011) containing bird images from 3333 classes. Each instance is also annotated with a human-interpretable attribute used during generation (e.g., crest color), yielding 3333 distinct values. We train the teacher using both class labels and concept annotations, and use m=10m=10.

Methods. We fix the gauge on unembeddings by centering them as in Eq. 3. In all experiments, we first train a reference teacher model by minimizing the cross-entropy loss on labeled data. We then compare three types of student models: KL\mathrm{KL}-students, trained to minimize dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} to the teacher distribution, L2L_{2}-students and L1L_{1}-students, trained to minimize dlogit2d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2} and ℒlogit1\mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathrm{logit}}, respectively. We use ResNet (He et al., 2016) and DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2023) as feature extractors for CIFAR and SUB, respectively. All architectural details, hyperparameter choices, and train–validation–test splits are reported in Appendix K. Teachers and students share the same architectures and representational dimensionality, except on CIFAR, where we use different ResNet sizes.

Metrics. We measure the representational similarity between students and teachers using mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}} and drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} computed on their embeddings, and distributional distance with dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} and dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}}. We report classification accuracy on ground-truth labels, denoted Acc(Y)(Y). On SUB, we additionally evaluate how well linear classifiers recover human-annotated concepts from the embeddings, reported as Acc​(C)\texttt{Acc}(C). We evaluate all metrics on the test set and average the results over 55 teacher seeds and 55 student seeds per teacher, reporting means and standard deviations. More details and results are provided in Appendix K.

5.1 Distillation with ℒlogit1\mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathrm{logit}} or dlogit2d^{2}_{\mathrm{logit}} yields more similar representations than dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}}

All teachers excel in label prediction on Synth, attaining the maximum Acc​(Y)\texttt{Acc}(Y) (Table 2). On SUB, they exhibit high accuracy for both labels and concepts (Table 2). Performance on CIFAR is moderate. The students, compatibly, score close to teachers in terms of Acc(Y)(Y) on all datasets, with students improving over the teachers on SUB. For Synth and SUB, we observe that L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} students display smaller dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} than the KL student, and for all datasets L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} students have lower dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} (even one order of magnitude below KL students in Synth and SUB, see Section K.3). In all datasets, we observe a drastic increase in similarity when minimizing ℒlogit1\mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathrm{logit}} and dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} rather than dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}}. L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} students reduce drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} by an order of magnitude compared to KL\mathrm{KL} students in Synth, while L2L_{2} reduces by two orders in CIFAR, and three orders of magnitude on SUB. Also, mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}} is always higher for L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, scoring (almost) perfectly on Synth and SUB and improving by more than 2020 pp on CIFAR. This results in more similar representations, as qualitatively displayed in Fig. 2 for the Synth dataset.

5.2 Distillation with ℒlogit1\mathcal{L}^{1}_{\mathrm{logit}} or dlogit2d^{2}_{\mathrm{logit}} recovers linear concepts of the teacher, while dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} does not

We experiment on SUB by training teachers to be (linearly) predictive of both labels and concepts from the embeddings. We observe that KL\mathrm{KL} students, while achieving relatively high values of mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}, have worse drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} than L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} students and fare extremely poorly on concept classification, scoring slightly above a random classifier (1/33≈0.031/33\approx 0.03). On the other hand, L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} students, while showing lower Acc​(Y)\texttt{Acc}(Y), improve over all other metrics. Optimal mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}} and lower drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} reflect also in higher Acc​(C)\texttt{Acc}(C) (below teacher by 1717 p.p. for L1L_{1}). This is also qualitatively visible in Fig. 1, where the 2​d2d LDA projection on 66 concept attributes shows high linear separability for the L1L_{1} student (on the left) but not for KL\mathrm{KL} student (on the right).

6 Discussion and Conclusion

Limitations. (i) As in prior works (Khemakhem et al., 2020b; Roeder et al., 2021; Nielsen et al., 2025), we assume that the number of labels exceeds the representation dimension plus one. This is satisfied for language models with large vocabularies, but may be restrictive in standard image-classification settings with few classes. In future work, we would thus like to do experiments on language models, where our assumptions are likely to be met. Extending our results to regimes where the number of labels is equal to, or smaller than, the representation dimension (Marconato et al., 2025) is another key next step. (ii) In our Definition 3.7, we assumed our models to be in general position (Assumption 3.5). This resembles the diversity assumption (Assumption 2.1), but it is stronger. Similar to diversity, it is satisfied with high probability for random vectors in high dimension (mm large) under mild conditions.

Notions of representational similarity. Our results show that having models whose distributions are close in KL divergence does not provide strong guarantees for linear representational similarity. If closeness in KL induces a robust notion of representational similarity, it is therefore likely to be of a different kind. Relatedly, Huh et al. (2024) report that standard linear similarity metrics reveal limited convergence, whereas a mutual kk-nearest-neighbor metric on representation space uncovers strong alignment across models. Other similarity notions are discussed in Appendix A.

Drivers of representational similarity. Our Theorem 3.3 implies weak linear representational similarity guarantees for KL, which is connected to the cross entropy loss (11); nonetheless, some works report empirical observations of linear representational similarity under the cross entropy loss—e.g., (Reizinger et al., 2025). There may thus be additional factors that drive the observed similarity, for example, learning dynamics in early phases of training (e.g.,  Frankle et al. (2020); Kapoor et al. (2025)), see also Appendix A.

Distillation and representational similarity. There is also a line of work on similarity-based knowledge distillation that explicitly matches hidden states between teacher and student, for example by aligning embedding spaces or internal features with auxiliary losses (Singh and Wang, 2024; Wang et al., 2023). Our analysis is complementary: rather than adding representational regularizers, we study how purely distributional objectives—KL divergence and our logit-based distance—control (or fail to control) linear representational similarity.

Conclusion. We showed that the logit distance is a metric between model distributions and, under a lower bound on conditional probabilities, can be controlled by the KL divergence. Building on this, we introduced the linear identifiability dissimilarity, tightly linked to the identifiability of the model family, and proved that logit distance upper-bounds both this dissimilarity and the mCCA between representations. Empirically, minimizing the logit distance yields student models whose representations are substantially more linearly similar to their teachers’ than when training with standard KL-based distillation.

Appendix A Additional Related Work

In this section we reference additional related work.

Measures of representational similarity and dissimilarity. Similar to our use of mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}, several prior works on representational similarity employ CCA-based measures [Raghu et al., 2017, Morcos et al., 2018] and only measure (dis)similarity between embeddings. Kornblith et al. [2019] introduce the CKA measure, invariant only to linear orthogonal transformations. Nielsen et al. [2025] also introduce a dissimilarity measure for our model class, d𝐟,𝐠d_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}. What constitutes the most appropriate measure of representational similarity remains an open question [Bansal et al., 2021], and existing approaches reflect different objectives and associated trade-offs Klabunde et al. [2025].

Other drivers of representational similarity. Ciernik et al. [2024] show that the training objective strongly impacts how consistently representational similarity generalizes across datasets. Li et al. [2025b] find that dataset and task overlap both correlate strongly with increased representational similarity, especially in combination. The role of early stages of training in shaping shared representational structure was investigated by [Frankle et al., 2020]. Braun et al. [2025] showed that enforcing robustness to parameter noise during training can force more aligned representations across runs.

Interpretable properties in model representations. A wealth of works studies learning concepts in weakly-supervised settings [Taeb et al., 2022, Marconato et al., 2023, Rajendran et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2025, Bortolotti et al., 2025, Goyal et al., 2025]. Our work differs in spirit from these, as we show which distillation schemes preserve already existing linearly encoded concepts in the teacher representations, especially when distributional equality cannot be guaranteed. The notion we propose of linearly encoded concepts shares some similarities to that of Rajendran et al. [2024], but we focus on probability distributions over categorical values instead of conceptual subspaces. Other interpretable properties can be linearly encoded in model representations, such as parallel directions in model unembeddings [Mikolov et al., 2013, Park et al., 2023] and relational linearity in model embeddings of text sentences [Hernandez et al., 2023, Marconato et al., 2025]. Both have also been shown to allowing steering model behavior [Hase et al., 2023, Stolfo et al., 2024]. We expect small values of dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} to preserve these properties as well, but we leave an in-depth analysis to future work.

Appendix B Definitions and background material

In this section, we recall useful mathematical definitions and results for later proofs of main paper claims.

B.1 Background on Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA)

Consider two random vectors 𝐗∈ℝm{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and 𝐘∈ℝm′{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{\prime}}. The first canonical variables are given by

(𝐚1,𝐛1)=argmax𝐚∈ℝm,𝐛∈ℝm′corr​(𝐚⋅𝐗,𝐛⋅𝐘)\displaystyle({\bm{\mathrm{a}}}_{1},{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}_{1})=\argmax_{{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{\prime}}}\mathrm{corr}({\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\cdot{\bm{\mathrm{X}}},{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}\cdot{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}) (24)

where corr\mathrm{corr} denotes the correlation coefficient. And we denote by

ρ1=max𝐚∈ℝm,𝐛∈ℝm′⁡corr⁡(𝐚⋅𝐗,𝐛⋅𝐘)\displaystyle\rho_{1}=\max_{{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{\prime}}}\mathrm{corr}({\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\cdot{\bm{\mathrm{X}}},{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}\cdot{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}) (25)

the first canonical correlation. The second and all further canonical variables and canonical correlations are defined similarly except that we restrict the maximum to the orthogonal complements of all previous canonical variables. There are a total of min⁡(m,m′)\min(m,m^{\prime}) canonical correlations. It can be shown that these correspond to the left and right singular vectors and the singular values of the matrix

𝚺𝐗𝐗−1/2𝚺𝐗𝐘𝚺𝐘𝐘−1/2\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}}^{-1/2}{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}}{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}}^{-1/2} (26)

where 𝚺𝐗𝐗{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}} and 𝚺𝐘𝐘{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}} are the covariance matrices of 𝐗{\bm{\mathrm{X}}} and 𝐘{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}} and

𝚺𝐗𝐘=𝔼⁡((𝐗−𝔼⁡(𝐗))​(𝐘−𝔼⁡(𝐘))⊤)\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}}=\mathbb{E}\left(({\bm{\mathrm{X}}}-\mathbb{E}({\bm{\mathrm{X}}}))({\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}-\mathbb{E}({\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}))^{\top}\right) (27)

the cross correlation. Clearly, this is invariant to linear transformations of the variables. For m=m′m=m^{\prime} We consider the mean CCA

mCCA=1m​∑i=1mρi.\displaystyle m_{\mathrm{CCA}}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\rho_{i}. (28)

Variables 𝐗{\bm{\mathrm{X}}} and 𝐘{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}} are linearly related iff mCCA=1m_{\mathrm{CCA}}=1. Sums of canonical correlations can be related to matrix norms through (26), e.g., by

∑i=1min⁡(m,m′)ρi2=Tr(𝚺𝐗𝐗−1/2𝚺𝐗𝐘𝚺𝐘𝐘−1𝚺𝐘𝐗𝚺𝐗𝐗−1/2).\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{\min(m,m^{\prime})}\rho_{i}^{2}=\tr\left({\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}}^{-1/2}{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}}{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{Y}}}{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}}{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}}^{-1/2}\right). (29)

B.2 Von Neumann’s trace inequality

For reference we state von Neumann’s trace inequality which is a bound for the trace of the product of two positive semi-definite matrices.

Theorem B.1 (Von Neumann’s trace inequality).

For positive semi-definite symmetric (or hermitian) matrices 𝐀,𝐁∈ℝm×m{\bm{\mathrm{A}}},{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} with eigenvalues a1≥a2≥…≥ama_{1}\geq a_{2}\geq\ldots\geq a_{m} and b1≥b2≥…≥bmb_{1}\geq b_{2}\geq\ldots\geq b_{m} the following bound holds

∑i=1mai​bm+1−i≤Tr⁡(𝐀𝐁)≤∑i=1mai​bi.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}b_{m+1-i}\leq\tr({\bm{\mathrm{A}}}{\bm{\mathrm{B}}})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}b_{i}. (30)

For any two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta that satisfy the diversity condition (Assumption 2.1) and such that

p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)=p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱),∀(𝐱,y)∈𝒳×𝒴,p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),\quad\forall({\bm{\mathrm{x}}},y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\,, (31)

𝐋~𝒥=(𝐠⁡(y~1)−𝐠⁡(y~)⋯𝐠⁡(y~m)−𝐠⁡(y~)),𝐋^𝒦=(𝐠⁡(y^1)−𝐠⁡(y^)⋯𝐠⁡(y^m)−𝐠⁡(y^))\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y}_{1})-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y})&\cdots&{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y}_{m})-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y})\end{pmatrix},\quad\hat{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{K}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\hat{y}_{1})-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\hat{y})&\cdots&{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\hat{y}_{m})-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\hat{y})\end{pmatrix} (32)

𝐋^𝒦=𝐋~𝒥​𝐎.\hat{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{K}}=\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{O}}}\,. (33)

𝐀\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{A}}} =𝐋^𝒦−⁣⊤𝐋^𝒦′⊤\displaystyle=\hat{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{K}}^{-\top}\hat{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{K}}^{{}^{\prime}\top} (46)

Appendix D Theoretical Material for first part of Section 3: How Logit Distance is Connected to Log Probabilities and Proof that it is a Metric

In this section we first show how the logit distance, dlogit​(p,p′)d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime}), from Definition 3.1 can be written as a difference between log probabilities of sets of distributions with only non-zero probabilities, Section D.1. We then show that logit distance is a proper metric, Section D.3.

D.1 Logit Distance in Terms of log Probabilities

We recall that we defined the logits of models from our model class as:

𝐮⁡(𝐱)=(𝐠​(y1)⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)𝐠​(yk)⊤​𝐟​(𝐱))\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{1})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{k})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\\ \end{pmatrix} (49)

We will show that the logit distance is equal to a difference of log probabilities as in the following result:

Lemma D.1.

Let p,p′p,p^{\prime}, be distributions generated by the model class Eq. 1, where mm is the dimension of the representations. Let N=(k−2m−1)N=\binom{k-2}{m-1}. When evaluating dlogit​(p,p′)d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime}), we have that

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖22=12​k​N​∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}‖(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))j∈𝒥‖22.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2kN}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\left\|\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\;.\end{split} (50)

where on the right we have a vector indexed with jj running over the set 𝒥\mathcal{J}.

We show the result in two steps: First we show that the logit distance can be written in terms of shifted logits, defined in the following way:

𝐮i​(𝐱)=(𝐠​(y1)⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)𝐠​(yk)⊤​𝐟​(𝐱))−𝐠​(yi)⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)​(11)\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{1})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{k})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\\ \end{pmatrix}-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \vdots\\ 1\end{pmatrix} (51)

Then we will show that the shifted logits are the same as a difference of log probabilities.

Proposition D.2.

The following relation holds

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖22=12​k​∑yi∈𝒴‖𝐮i​(𝐱)−𝐮i′​(𝐱)‖22=12​k​(k−2m−1)​∑yi∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{yi},|𝒥|=m∑j∈𝒥(ui​(𝐱)j−ui′​(𝐱)j)2.\displaystyle||{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||^{2}_{2}=\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{y_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}}||{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||^{2}_{2}=\frac{1}{2k\binom{k-2}{m-1}}\sum_{y_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{y_{i}\},\,|\mathcal{J}|=m}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\left(u_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}-u^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}\right)^{2}. (52)
Remark D.3.

The first identity is essentially a version of the well-known identity

𝔼​(𝐗−𝐗′)2=2​V​a​r​(𝐗)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}({\bm{\mathrm{X}}}-{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}^{\prime})^{2}=2\mathrm{Var}({\bm{\mathrm{X}}}) (53)

holding true for two independent copies 𝐗{\bm{\mathrm{X}}} and 𝐗′{\bm{\mathrm{X}}}^{\prime} of a random variable.

Proof.

We observe that since we assume that the unembeddings 𝐠⁡(yi){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}) and 𝐠′​(yi){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i}) are centred we get

(𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱))⋅(11)=∑i=1k𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yi)−𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yi)=𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​(∑i=1k𝐠⁡(yi))−𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​(∑i=1k𝐠′​(yi))=0.\displaystyle\left({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \vdots\\ 1\end{pmatrix}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i})={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})\right)-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i})\right)=0. (54)

∑i=1k∥𝐮i​(𝐱)−𝐮i′​(𝐱)∥2=k​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2+k​∑i=1k((u⁡(𝐱))i−(u′​(𝐱))i)2=2​k​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}=k\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}+k\sum_{i=1}^{k}((u({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))_{i}-(u^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))_{i})^{2}=2k\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2} (56)

and therefore the first relation. For the second relation we first note that by definition

ui​(𝐱)i−ui′​(𝐱)i=(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yi)−𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yi))−(𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yi)−𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yi))=0.\displaystyle u_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{i}-u^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{i}=({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}))-({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i}))=0. (57)

Then we use that each index j≠ij\neq i appears in (k−2m−1)\binom{k-2}{m-1} subsets of size mm not containing index ii. Indeed, we have to select m−1m-1 remaining points of the set of size mm from k−2k-2 options (ii and jj are removed from the kk options). Therefore, for each pivot yiy_{i}

∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{yi},|𝒥|=m∑j∈𝒥(ui​(𝐱)j−ui′​(𝐱)j)2=(k−2m−1)​∑j≠i(ui​(𝐱)j−ui′​(𝐱)j)2=(k−2m−1)​∑j=1k(ui​(𝐱)j−ui′​(𝐱)j)2=(k−2m−1)​∥𝐮i​(𝐱)−𝐮i′​(𝐱)∥2.\displaystyle\begin{split}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{y_{i}\},\,|\mathcal{J}|=m}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\left(u_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}-u^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}\right)^{2}&=\binom{k-2}{m-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\left(u_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}-u^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}\right)^{2}\\ &=\binom{k-2}{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left(u_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}-u^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{j}\right)^{2}\\ &=\binom{k-2}{m-1}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}.\end{split} (58)

This implies the second part of (52) by summing over yiy_{i}.

∎

We recall that the matrix of shifted unembeddings constructed from 𝐠~\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} using a subset of mm labels 𝒥={y1,…,ym}⊆𝒴∖{y~}\mathcal{J}=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{m}\}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}:

𝐠~​(y):=𝐠⁡(y)−𝐠⁡(y~),𝐋~𝒥:=(𝐠~​(y1)⋯𝐠~​(ym))∈ℝm×m.\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y):={\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y}),\quad\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}:=\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{1})&\cdots&\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{m})\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\,. (59)

With this definition we can also write the following result.

Lemma D.4.

Let N=(k−2m−1)N=\binom{k-2}{m-1}. When evaluating dlogit​(p,p′)d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime}) on distributions, p,p′p,p^{\prime}, generated by the model class Eq. 1, where mm is the dimension of the representations, we have that:

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖2=12​k​N​∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}‖𝐋~𝒥⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖22\displaystyle||{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||^{2}=\frac{1}{2kN}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2} (60)
Proof.

This is since taking the entries of the shifted logits 𝐮i​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) corresponding to the mm labels from 𝒥\mathcal{J}, is the same as 𝐋~𝒥⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}). ∎

Lemma D.5.

When evaluating dlogit​(p,p′)d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime}) on distributions, p,p′p,p^{\prime}, generated by the model class Eq. 1, where mm is the dimension of the representations, we have that:

‖𝐋~𝒥⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖2=‖(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))j∈𝒥‖2\displaystyle\begin{split}&\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}=\left\|\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\right\|_{2}\end{split} (61)

where on the right we have a vector with entries indexed by jj running over the set 𝒥\mathcal{J}.

Proof.

We consider first the definition of the norm:

‖𝐋~𝒥⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖22\displaystyle\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2} =∑j=1m(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yj)−𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yj)−𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y~)+𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(y~))2\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{j})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{j})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y})+{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(\tilde{y}))^{2} (62)

We then consider each term of the sum, and see that if we both add and subtract a normalization term for each model, then the value will be unchanged. That is, we have

𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yj)−𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y~)=log⁡(exp⁡(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yj)))−log⁡(exp⁡(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y~)))−log⁡(∑ynexp⁡(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yn)))+log⁡(∑ynexp⁡(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yn)))=log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱))\displaystyle\begin{split}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{j})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y})&=\log(\exp({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{j})))-\log(\exp({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\tilde{y})))\\ &\quad-\log\left(\sum_{y_{n}}\exp({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{n}))\right)+\log\left(\sum_{y_{n}}\exp({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{n}))\right)\\ &=\log(p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))-\log(p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))\end{split} (63)

And thus we see that

‖𝐋~𝒥⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖22\displaystyle\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2} =∑j=1m(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱))−log⁡(p′​(yj|𝐱))+log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)))2\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(\log(p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))-\log(p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))-\log(p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))+\log(p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})))^{2} (64)
=∑j=1m(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))2\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)^{2} (65)
=‖(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))j∈𝒥‖22.\displaystyle=\left\|\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (66)

D.2 Connection between the Logit Distance and the Aitchison Distance

In this section we show how the Logit Distance is related to the Aitchison distance. The Aitchison distance takes inputs from the hull of the simplex for CC values defined as,

ΔC−1={𝐳={z1,…,zC}|zi>0,i=1,…,C,∑i=1Czi=1},\displaystyle\Delta^{C-1}=\left\{{\bm{\mathrm{z}}}=\{z_{1},...,z_{C}\}|z_{i}>0,i=1,...,C,\sum_{i=1}^{C}z_{i}=1\right\}\;, (67)

and the distance is defined for 𝐳,𝐰∈ΔC−1{\bm{\mathrm{z}}},{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}\in\Delta^{C-1} as

da​(𝐳,𝐰)=12​C​∑i=1C∑j=1C(log⁡(zjzi)−log⁡(wjwi))2.\displaystyle d_{a}({\bm{\mathrm{z}}},{\bm{\mathrm{w}}})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2C}\sum_{i=1}^{C}\sum_{j=1}^{C}\left(\log\left(\frac{z_{j}}{z_{i}}\right)-\log\left(\frac{w_{j}}{w_{i}}\right)\right)^{2}}\;. (68)

Since our models always assign non-zero probabilities and sum to 11, the probabilities are in the hull of the simplex. This means that the squared distance between logits is the same as the Aitchison distance between the probabilities for a given input, 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}.

Proposition D.6.

Let p,p′p,p^{\prime} be sets of probabilties from our model class and let 𝐮​(𝐱),𝐮′​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) be the logits. Then for each 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} we have

∥𝐮(𝐱)−𝐮′(𝐱)∥22=da2(p(⋅|𝐱),p′(⋅|𝐱)).\displaystyle\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2}=d_{a}^{2}(p(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),p^{\prime}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))\;. (69)
Proof.

We see that

(𝐮i​(𝐱)−𝐮i′​(𝐱))j=𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yj)−𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yi)−𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yj)+𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yi)=log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱))log⁡(p⁡(yi|𝐱))−log⁡(p′​(yj|𝐱))log⁡(p′​(yi|𝐱)).\displaystyle\left({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)_{j}={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{j})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{j})+{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i})=\frac{\log(p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}{\log(p(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}-\frac{\log(p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}{\log(p^{\prime}(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}\;. (70)

Which means that

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖22\displaystyle\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2} =12​k​∑yi∈𝒴‖𝐮i​(𝐱)−𝐮i′​(𝐱)‖22\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{y_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}}||{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||^{2}_{2} (71)
=12​k​∑i=1k∑j=1k(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱))log⁡(p⁡(yi|𝐱))−log⁡(p′​(yj|𝐱))log⁡(p′​(yi|𝐱)))2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left(\frac{\log(p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}{\log(p(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}-\frac{\log(p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}{\log(p^{\prime}(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}\right)^{2} (72)
=da2(p(⋅|𝐱),p′(⋅|𝐱))\displaystyle=d_{a}^{2}(p(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),p^{\prime}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})) (73)

∎

D.3 The Logit Distance is a Metric

In this section we provide a full proof that the logit distance is a metric. We will begin by defining a distance between sets of probability distributions which are not necessarily from our model class:

Definition D.7.

Let p,p′p,p^{\prime} be two sets of conditional distributions with kk labels and only non-zero probabilities. Let m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, N=(k−2m−1)N=\binom{k-2}{m-1}. The shifted log-likelihood distance for p,p′p,p^{\prime} is defined as:

dLLDm​(p,p′)=12​k​N​∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))j‖2\displaystyle d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2kN}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\left\|\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)_{j}\right\|_{2} (74)
Theorem D.8.

For any m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, the function from Definition D.7 is a metric (which can have infinite value) between sets of conditional distributions, p,p′p,p^{\prime}, over kk labels with non-zero probabilities.

Proof.

We will show that Definition D.7 is a metric. That is,

  1. i

    it is non-negative, dLLDm​(p,p′)≥0d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})\geq 0, and zero only when all distributions are equal, dLLDm​(p,p′)=0⇔p=p′d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})=0\iff p=p^{\prime}.

  2. ii

    It is symmetric, dLLDm​(p,p′)=dLLDm​(p′,p)d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})=d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p^{\prime},p).

  3. iii

    It satisfies the triangle inequality, dLLDm​(p1,p2)≤dLLDm​(p1,p3)+dLLDm​(p3,p2)d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p_{1},p_{2})\leq d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p_{1},p_{3})+d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p_{3},p_{2}).

W.r.t. i) we see that Eq. 74 is non-negative, since it is a norm. We will show that if p=p′p=p^{\prime}, then dLLDm​(p,p′)=0d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})=0: When p=p′p=p^{\prime}, p⁡(yj|𝐱)=p′​(yj|𝐱)p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) for any choice of {yj}j=0m\{y_{j}\}_{j=0}^{m}, therefore dLLDm​(p,p′)=0d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})=0. We will now show that if dLLDm​(p,p′)=0d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})=0 then p=p′p=p^{\prime}: Assume dLLDm​(p,p′)=0d^{m}_{\mathrm{LLD}}(p,p^{\prime})=0, that is:

12​k​N​∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))j‖=0\displaystyle\frac{1}{2kN}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\left\|\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)_{j}\right\|=0 (75)

Since the norm is always non-negative, this means that

𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖(log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))j‖=0,∀{yj}j=0m⊆𝒴\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\left\|\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)_{j}\right\|=0,\;\forall\{y_{j}\}_{j=0}^{m}\subseteq\mathcal{Y} (76)

Which means that for all choices of {yj}j=0m⊆𝒴\{y_{j}\}_{j=0}^{m}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}, we have that each entry in the vector (log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)))j\left(\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)-\log\left(\frac{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right)\right)_{j} is zero almost everywhere33 3 Almost everywhere, also abbreviated a.e.: Everywhere except on some null-set, that is except on a set with measure zero..

That is, we have

log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱))\displaystyle\log(p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))-\log(p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})) −log⁡(p′​(yj|𝐱))+log⁡(p′​(y~|𝐱))=0\displaystyle-\log(p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))+\log(p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))=0 (77)
log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p⁡(y~|𝐱))\displaystyle\log(p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))-\log(p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})) =log⁡(p′​(yj|𝐱))−log⁡(p′​(y~|𝐱))\displaystyle=\log(p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))-\log(p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})) (78)
log⁡(p⁡(yj|𝐱)p⁡(y~|𝐱))\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right) =log⁡(p′​(yj|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱))\displaystyle=\log\left(\frac{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\right) (79)
p⁡(yj|𝐱)p⁡(y~|𝐱)\displaystyle\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})} =p′​(yj|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)\displaystyle=\frac{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})} (80)

for all yj,y~∈𝒴y_{j},\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}. Now since p⁡(yi|𝐱)p(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) and p′​(yi|𝐱)p^{\prime}(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) are probability distributions, we have that

1p⁡(y~|𝐱)=∑j=0cp⁡(yj|𝐱)p⁡(y~|𝐱)=∑j=0cp′​(yj|𝐱)p′​(y~|𝐱)=1p′​(y~|𝐱)\displaystyle\frac{1}{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}=\sum_{j=0}^{c}\frac{p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}=\sum_{j=0}^{c}\frac{p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}=\frac{1}{p^{\prime}(\tilde{y}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})} (81)

which means that Eq. 80 gives us

p⁡(yj|𝐱)=p′​(yj|𝐱),∀yj∈𝒴\displaystyle p(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=p^{\prime}(y_{j}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),\forall y_{j}\in\mathcal{Y} (82)

and almost everywhere w.r.t. 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} thus, p=p′p=p^{\prime} a.e..

W.r.t. ii) Eq. 74 is symmetric, since the norm is symmetric.

We are now ready to prove the theorem:

Theorem D.9.

For any two models from our model class, the logit distance from Definition 3.1 is a metric between their sets of distributions, p,p′p,p^{\prime}.
