Appendix E Theoretical Material for Section 3.1: Bounding logit difference by the KL divergence

E.1 Assumption 3.2 guarantees that embeddings and unembeddings are bounded

We notice that requiring that a model (𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta is τ\tau-lower bounded (Assumption 3.2) is equivalent to ask that embeddings and unembeddings are bounded. We remark that the unembeddings are always bounded when the number of labels is finite. We first show that bounded 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} implies lower bounded probability. For this, notice that:

p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱)\displaystyle p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) =exp⁡(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y))∑y′∈𝒴exp⁡(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y′))\displaystyle=\frac{\exp({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y))}{\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}\exp({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y^{\prime}))} (98)
≥exp(−||𝐟(𝐱)||⋅maxy∈𝒴||𝐠(y)||)k​exp⁡(‖𝐟⁡(𝐱)‖⋅maxy∈𝒴⁡‖𝐠⁡(y)‖)\displaystyle\geq\frac{\exp\big({-||{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||\cdot\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}||{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)||}\big)}{k\exp\big({||{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||\cdot\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}||{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)||}\big)} (99)
=miny∈𝒴⁡exp(−2||𝐟(𝐱)||⋅||𝐠(y)||)k\displaystyle=\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{\exp\big({-2||{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||\cdot||{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)||}\big)}{k} (100)
≥ess​inf𝐱∈supp⁡(p𝐱)⁡miny∈𝒴​exp(−2||𝐟(𝐱)||⋅||𝐠(y)||)k.\displaystyle\geq\essinf_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathrm{supp}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}})}\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{\exp{\big(-2||{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||\cdot||{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)||\big)}}{k}. (101)

The last quantity is finite for bounded 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} and Assumption 3.2 holds for

τ=ess​inf𝐱∈supp⁡(p𝐱)⁡miny∈𝒴​p​(y∣𝐱).\tau=\essinf_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathrm{supp}(p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})}\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}). (102)

On the contrary, if embeddings or unembeddings are not bounded, Eq. 12 cannot be satisfied for τ>0\tau>0. Since we only consider a finite number of labels we focus on unbounded embeddings. Assume the embeddings are unbounded. Then there is a sequence 𝐱i{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i} so that ∥𝐟⁡(𝐱i)∥→∞\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})\rVert\to\infty. By the diversity assumption we find that

inf𝐯∈Sm−1maxy,y¯∈𝒴⁡(𝐠⁡(y)−𝐠⁡(y¯))​𝐯≥α>0\displaystyle\inf_{{\bm{\mathrm{v}}}\in S^{m-1}}\max_{y,\bar{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\left({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\bar{y})\right){\bm{\mathrm{v}}}\geq\alpha>0 (103)

for some α\alpha. Indeed, the left hand side is a continuous function on a compact domain and pointwise positive. Thus we find a sequence yiy_{i}, y¯i\bar{y}_{i} such that

𝐟⁡(𝐱i)⋅(𝐠⁡(yi)−𝐠⁡(y¯i))=𝐟⁡(𝐱i)⋅maxy,y¯∈𝒴⁡(𝐠⁡(y)−𝐠⁡(y¯))≥α⁡∥𝐟⁡(𝐱i)∥.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})\cdot\left({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\bar{y}_{i})\right)={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})\cdot\max_{y,\bar{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\left({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\bar{y})\right)\geq\alpha\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})\rVert. (104)

This implies that

p𝐟,𝐠​(y¯i|𝐱i)=p𝐟,𝐠​(yi|𝐱i)​e−𝐟​(𝐱i)⊤​(𝐠⁡(yi)−𝐠⁡(y¯i))≤1⋅e−α​∥𝐟⁡(𝐱i)∥→0\displaystyle p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\bar{y}_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})=p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}({y}_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})e^{-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})^{\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})-{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(\bar{y}_{i})\right)}\leq 1\cdot e^{-\alpha\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}_{i})\rVert}\to 0 (105)

as i→∞i\to\infty. Therefore, probabilities cannot be τ\tau-bounded for any τ>0\tau>0.

E.2 Bounding logit distance with KL divergence

In this section, we start by considering two generic probability distributions 𝐩=(p1,…,pd){\bm{\mathrm{p}}}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{d}) and 𝐪=(q1,…,qd){\bm{\mathrm{q}}}=(q_{1},\ldots,q_{d}) with dd outcomes, such that pi,qi≥0p_{i},q_{i}\geq 0. We show how to provide bounds for the logit differences ∑i(log⁡(pi)−log⁡(qi))2\sum_{i}(\log(p_{i})-\log(q_{i}))^{2} in terms of the KL-divergence ∑ipi​log⁡(pi/qi)\sum_{i}p_{i}\log(p_{i}/q_{i}) While these bounds are generally standard, we could not locate the required bounds in the literature and therefore provide complete proofs here.

Let us first clarify that this is not generally possible. We consider the two probability distributions with two outcomes (d=2d=2) whose probabilities are given by (p1,p2)=(τ,1−τ)(p_{1},p_{2})=(\tau,1-\tau) and (q1,q2)=(τ2,1−τ2)(q_{1},q_{2})=(\tau^{2},1-\tau^{2}) for some 0≤τ<10\leq\tau<1. Then, on one hand, we find

∑i(log⁡(pi)−log⁡(qi))2≥log⁡(τ)2\displaystyle\sum_{i}(\log(p_{i})-\log(q_{i}))^{2}\geq\log(\tau)^{2} (106)

and on the other hand

KL(𝐩||𝐪)=τlog(τ/τ2)+(1−τ)log((1−τ)/(1−τ2))≤τ|log(τ)|.\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}})=\tau\log(\tau/\tau^{2})+(1-\tau)\log((1-\tau)/(1-\tau^{2}))\leq\tau|\log(\tau)|. (107)

Since the former diverges as τ→0\tau\to 0 while the latter converges to 00 it is generally not possible to bound the squared logit difference by a function of the KL-divergence only. This is also the root of the observation that small KL-divergence between models in general does not imply similar representations [Nielsen et al., 2025].

We therefore consider assuming a lower bound on pip_{i} for such a bound. We first assume in addition that qiq_{i} is also lower bounded. Before stating the bound in this case we provide one auxiliary lemma that we will need in the proof.

Lemma E.1.

For τ≤1/3\tau\leq 1/3 the following bound holds for all x≥τx\geq\tau

log⁡(x)2≤4​log⁡(τ)2​(x​log⁡(x)−x+1).\displaystyle\log(x)^{2}\leq 4\log(\tau)^{2}(x\log(x)-x+1). (108)
Proof.

We define the function Φ:ℝ+∖{1}→ℝ\Phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\setminus\{1\}\to\mathbb{R} given by

Φ⁡(x)=log⁡(x)2x​log⁡(x)−x+1.\displaystyle\Phi(x)=\frac{\log(x)^{2}}{x\log(x)-x+1}. (109)

We observe that the function at thet denominator x→x​log⁡(x)−x+1x\to x\log(x)-x+1 is convex, minimized at x=1x=1, and non-negative on ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} and thus Φ\Phi is well defined. We notice that Φ\Phi can be extended to a continuous function at 11 by setting Φ⁡(1)=2\Phi(1)=2. To prove the lemma we need to show that Φ⁡(x)≤4​log⁡(τ)2\Phi(x)\leq 4\log(\tau)^{2} for x≥τx\geq\tau. We will proceed in two steps: First we show that Φ\Phi is non-increasing and then we bound Φ⁡(τ)\Phi(\tau). To show that Φ\Phi is non-increasing we will need the following auxiliary fact: The function Ψ:ℝ+→ℝ\Psi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R} given by

Ψ⁡(x)=log⁡(x)−1+1x−log⁡(x)22\displaystyle\Psi(x)=\log(x)-1+\frac{1}{x}-\frac{\log(x)^{2}}{2} (110)

is decreasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty) and satisfies Ψ⁡(1)=0\Psi(1)=0, so in particular Ψ⁡(x)≥0\Psi(x)\geq 0 for x≤1x\leq 1 and Ψ⁡(x)≤0\Psi(x)\leq 0 for x≥1x\geq 1. To show this we note that

Ψ′​(x)=1x−1x2−log⁡(x)x=−1x2​(x​log⁡(x)−x+1)≤0.\displaystyle\Psi^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}-\frac{\log(x)}{x}=-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\left(x\log(x)-x+1\right)\leq 0. (111)

Now we calculate Φ′\Phi^{\prime} using (log⁡(x)​x−x+1)′=log⁡(x)(\log(x)x-x+1)^{\prime}=\log(x) and find

Φ′​(x)=2​log⁡(x)x​(x​log⁡(x)−x+1)−log⁡(x)2⋅log⁡(x)(x​log⁡(x)−x+1)2=2(x​log⁡(x)−x+1)2​log⁡(x)​(log⁡(x)−1+1x−log⁡(x)22)=2(x​log⁡(x)−x+1)2​log⁡(x)​Ψ​(x)≤0\displaystyle\begin{split}\Phi^{\prime}(x)=\frac{2\frac{\log(x)}{x}\left(x\log(x)-x+1\right)-\log(x)^{2}\cdot\log(x)}{\left(x\log(x)-x+1\right)^{2}}&=\frac{2}{\left(x\log(x)-x+1\right)^{2}}\log(x)\left(\log(x)-1+\frac{1}{x}-\frac{\log(x)^{2}}{2}\right)\\ &=\frac{2}{\left(x\log(x)-x+1\right)^{2}}\log(x)\Psi(x)\leq 0\end{split} (112)

where we used that log⁡(x)\log(x) and Ψ⁡(x)\Psi(x) both change their sign at x=1x=1 so the product is always non-positive. Therefore we conclude that

supx∈[τ,τ−1]∖{1}Φ⁡(x)=Φ⁡(τ)=log⁡(τ)2τ​log⁡(τ)−τ+1≤4​log⁡(τ)2\displaystyle\sup_{x\in[\tau,\tau^{-1}]\setminus\{1\}}\Phi(x)=\Phi(\tau)=\frac{\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau\log(\tau)-\tau+1}\leq 4\log(\tau)^{2} (113)

where we used τ​log⁡(τ)−τ+1≥1/3​log⁡(1/3)−1/3+1≥1/4\tau\log(\tau)-\tau+1\geq 1/3\log(1/3)-1/3+1\geq 1/4 for τ≤1/3\tau\leq 1/3 in the last step. ∎

We can now state and prove the upper bound.

Lemma E.2.

Let 𝐩{\bm{\mathrm{p}}} and 𝐪{\bm{\mathrm{q}}} be two probability distributions satisfying pi≥τp_{i}\geq\tau and qi≥τq_{i}\geq\tau for all ii and some 0<τ≤1/30<\tau\leq 1/3. Then

∑i(log(pi)−log(qi))2≤4​log⁡(τ)2τKL(𝐩||𝐪).\displaystyle\sum_{i}(\log(p_{i})-\log(q_{i}))^{2}\leq\frac{4\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}}). (114)
Remark E.3.

The bound is tight up to the logarithmic terms. Indeed, consider 𝐩=(2​τ,1−2​τ){\bm{\mathrm{p}}}=(2\tau,1-2\tau) and 𝐪=(τ,1−τ){\bm{\mathrm{q}}}=(\tau,1-\tau). Then the left hand side is bigger than log⁡(2)2\log(2)^{2} while the KL-divergence of these two distributions is bounded by log⁡(2)​τ\log(2)\tau.

Proof.

We write pi=xi​qip_{i}=x_{i}q_{i}. By assumption, pi=xi​qi≥τp_{i}=x_{i}q_{i}\geq\tau, which means that xi≥τqi≥τx_{i}\geq\frac{\tau}{q_{i}}\geq\tau. Also, xi=piqi≤1qi≤1τx_{i}=\frac{p_{i}}{q_{i}}\leq\frac{1}{q_{i}}\leq\frac{1}{\tau}. So we have xi∈[τ,τ−1]x_{i}\in[\tau,\tau^{-1}]. The starting point is to rewrite the KL-divergence as follows

KL(𝐩||𝐪)=∑ipilog(pi/qi)=∑iqi(xilog(xi)−xi+1).\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}})=\sum_{i}p_{i}\log(p_{i}/q_{i})=\sum_{i}q_{i}(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1). (115)

Here we used in the last step that ∑iqi​xi=∑ipi=1=∑iqi\sum_{i}q_{i}x_{i}=\sum_{i}p_{i}=1=\sum_{i}q_{i}. Recall that the function x→x​log⁡(x)−x+1x\to x\log(x)-x+1 is convex, minimized at x=1x=1, and non-negative. We apply (108) from Lemma E.1 to control

∑i(log⁡(pi)−log⁡(qi))2=∑ilog⁡(xi)2≤4​log⁡(τ)2​∑i(xi​log⁡(xi)−xi+1)≤4log(τ)2∑iqiτ(xilog(xi)−xi+1)=4​log⁡(τ)2τKL(𝐩||𝐪).\displaystyle\begin{split}\sum_{i}(\log(p_{i})-\log(q_{i}))^{2}&=\sum_{i}\log(x_{i})^{2}\leq 4\log(\tau)^{2}\sum_{i}(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1)\\ &\leq 4\log(\tau)^{2}\sum_{i}\frac{q_{i}}{\tau}(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1)=\frac{4\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}}).\end{split} (116)

∎

We can similarly show a slightly weaker bound without assuming that 𝐪{\bm{\mathrm{q}}} is lower bounded.

Lemma E.4.

Let 𝐩{\bm{\mathrm{p}}} and 𝐪{\bm{\mathrm{q}}} be two probability distributions satisfying pi≥τp_{i}\geq\tau for all ii and some 0<τ≤1/30<\tau\leq 1/3. Then

∑i(log(pi)−log(qi))2≤12​log⁡(τ)2τKL(𝐩||𝐪)+9τ2KL(𝐩||𝐪)2.\displaystyle\sum_{i}(\log(p_{i})-\log(q_{i}))^{2}\leq\frac{12\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}})+\frac{9}{\tau^{2}}\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}})^{2}. (117)
Remark E.5.

The second term can not be avoided. Note that for 𝐩=(τ,1−τ){\bm{\mathrm{p}}}=(\tau,1-\tau) and 𝐪=(ε,1−ε){\bm{\mathrm{q}}}=(\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon) we find

limε→0∑i(log⁡(pi)−log⁡(qi))2log⁡(ε)2=1\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{\sum_{i}(\log(p_{i})-\log(q_{i}))^{2}}{\log(\varepsilon)^{2}}=1 (118)

while

limε→0KL⁡(𝐩,𝐪)|log⁡(ε)|=τ.\displaystyle\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}},{\bm{\mathrm{q}}})}{|\log(\varepsilon)|}=\tau. (119)
Proof.

As before we write pi=xi​qip_{i}=x_{i}q_{i} but in contrast to before xix_{i} is not upper bounded but only satisfies xi≥pi≥τx_{i}\geq p_{i}\geq\tau. The main idea is to control log⁡(xi)2\log(x_{i})^{2} separately, when 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} is large we use a new bound based on a similar approach while we can apply the approach from before when 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} is small because this lower bounds qiq_{i}. We start with the former. Note that for x≥3x\geq 3 we find

log⁡(x)​x3≤x​log⁡(x)−x+1.\displaystyle\frac{\log(x)x}{3}\leq x\log(x)-x+1. (120)

Indeed, note that for x=3x=3

23​x​log⁡(x)−x+1=23⋅3⋅log⁡(3)−3+1>0\displaystyle\frac{2}{3}x\log(x)-x+1=\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3\cdot\log(3)-3+1>0 (121)

and

(23​x​log⁡(x)−x+1)′=23​log⁡(x)+23−1≥13\displaystyle\left(\frac{2}{3}x\log(x)-x+1\right)^{\prime}=\frac{2}{3}\log(x)+\frac{2}{3}-1\geq\frac{1}{3} (122)

for x≥3x\geq 3. This implies that

∑i:xi>3log(xi)2i≤∑i:xi>3(3xixi​log⁡(xi)3)2≤∑i:xi>3(3​piτ​xi(xilog(xi)−xi+1))2≤9τ2​∑i(qi​(xi​log⁡(xi)−xi+1))2≤9τ2(∑iqi(xilog(xi)−xi+1))2=9τ2KL(𝐩||𝐪)2.\displaystyle\begin{split}\sum_{i:\,x_{i}>3}\log(x_{i})^{2}_{i}&\leq\sum_{i:x_{i}>3}\left(\frac{3}{x_{i}}\frac{x_{i}\log(x_{i})}{3}\right)^{2}\\ &\leq\sum_{i:x_{i}>3}\left(\frac{3p_{i}}{\tau x_{i}}(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1)\right)^{2}\\ &\leq\frac{9}{\tau^{2}}\sum_{i}\left(q_{i}(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1)\right)^{2}\\ &\leq\frac{9}{\tau^{2}}\left(\sum_{i}q_{i}(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1)\right)^{2}=\frac{9}{\tau^{2}}\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}})^{2}.\end{split} (123)

Here we used in the last step that all terms in the sum are non-negative which implies that all cross terms in the expansion of the square of the sum are non-negative.

We now consider the indices ii so that xi<3x_{i}<3. Note that qi=pi/xi≥τ/3q_{i}=p_{i}/x_{i}\geq\tau/3. Therefore we obtain using xi≥τx_{i}\geq\tau and (108)

∑i:xi≤3log(𝐱)2i≤4log(τ)2∑i:xi≤3(xilog(xi)−xi+1)≤4log(τ)2∑i:xi≤3qiτ/3(xilog(xi)−xi+1)≤12​log⁡(τ)2τ∑iqi(xilog(xi)−xi+1)=12​log⁡(τ)2τKL(𝐩||𝐪).\displaystyle\begin{split}\sum_{i:x_{i}\leq 3}\log({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{2}_{i}&\leq 4\log(\tau)^{2}\sum_{i:x_{i}\leq 3}\left(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1\right)\\ &\leq 4\log(\tau)^{2}\sum_{i:x_{i}\leq 3}\frac{q_{i}}{\tau/3}\left(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1\right)\\ &\leq\frac{12\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}\sum_{i}{q_{i}}\left(x_{i}\log(x_{i})-x_{i}+1\right)=\frac{12\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}\mathrm{KL}({\bm{\mathrm{p}}}||{\bm{\mathrm{q}}}).\end{split} (124)

Combining (123) and (124) ends the proof. ∎

From these results it is straightforward to relate 𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yi){\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}) and 𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yi){\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i}).

Theorem E.6.

For two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta, denote with 𝐮⁡(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) and 𝐮′​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) the model logits 𝐮i​(𝐱)=𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yi){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}_{i}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}) and (𝐮′​(𝐱))i=𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yi)({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))_{i}={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i}). Fix a point 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}. Assume that miny∈𝒴⁡p𝐟,𝐠​(y|𝐱)≥τ\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\geq\tau. Then

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|^{2} ≤12​log⁡(τ)2τKL(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅|𝐱)||p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱))+9τ2KL(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅|𝐱)||p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱))2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{12\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}\mathrm{KL}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))+\frac{9}{\tau^{2}}\mathrm{KL}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))^{2}. (125)

If in addition miny∈𝒴⁡p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y|𝐱)≥τ\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\geq\tau then

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|^{2} ≤4​log⁡(τ)2τKL(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅|𝐱)||p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱)).\displaystyle\leq\frac{4\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}\mathrm{KL}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})). (126)
Proof.

We note that by (1)

𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y)=log⁡(p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱))+log⁡(∑y′∈𝒴e𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y′))\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)=\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)+\log\left(\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}e^{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y^{\prime})}\right) (127)

Using that 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} is centred we find

0=1k​∑y′∈𝒴𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y)=1k​∑y∈𝒴(log⁡(p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱))+log⁡(∑y′∈𝒴e𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y′)))=log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯+log⁡(∑y′∈𝒴e𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y′)).\displaystyle 0=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\left(\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)+\log\left(\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}e^{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y^{\prime})}\right)\right)=\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}+\log\left(\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}}e^{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y^{\prime})}\right). (128)

Where log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)} denote the mean over y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. We infer that

𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y)=log⁡(p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱))−log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)=\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)-\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}. (129)

Now we can conclude that

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖2=∑y∈𝒴(𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(y)−𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(y))2=∑y∈𝒴(log⁡(p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱))−log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯−log⁡(p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱))+log(p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅∣𝐱))¯)2=∑y∈𝒴(log⁡(p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱))−log⁡(p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱)))2+|𝒴|​(log(p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅∣𝐱))¯−log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯)2+2(log(p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅∣𝐱))¯−log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯)∑y∈𝒴(log(p𝐟,𝐠(y∣𝐱))−log(p𝐟′,𝐠′(y∣𝐱)))=∑y∈𝒴(log⁡(p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱))−log⁡(p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱)))2+|𝒴|​(log(p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅∣𝐱))¯−log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯)2−2​|𝒴|​(log(p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅∣𝐱))¯−log(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅∣𝐱))¯)2≤∑y∈𝒴(log⁡(p𝐟,𝐠​(y∣𝐱))−log⁡(p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y∣𝐱)))2.\displaystyle\begin{split}\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|^{2}&=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)-{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y))^{2}\\ &=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\left(\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)-\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}-\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)+\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}\right)^{2}\\ &=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\left(\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)-\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right)^{2}+|\mathcal{Y}|\left(\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}-\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}\right)^{2}\\ &\quad+2\left(\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}-\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}\right)\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\left(\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)-\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right)\\ &=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\left(\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)-\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right)^{2}+|\mathcal{Y}|\left(\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}-\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}\right)^{2}\\ &\quad-2|\mathcal{Y}|\left(\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}-\overline{\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)}\right)^{2}\\ &\leq\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\left(\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)-\log\left(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right)^{2}.\end{split} (130)

The last steps mirror the computation for showing that the squared norm is larger than the variance of a random variable. Now we can apply Lemma E.4 to conclude (125) and Lemma E.2 to get (126). ∎

We can integrate the previous result over 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}} to relate the mean logit difference to the cross entropy loss.

Corollary E.7.

For two models (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta, denote with 𝐮⁡(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) and 𝐮′​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) the model logits u​(𝐱)i=𝐟​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠​(yi)u({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{i}={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}) and u′​(𝐱)i=𝐟′​(𝐱)⊤​𝐠′​(yi)u^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})_{i}={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i}). Assume that for p𝐱p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}} almost every 𝐱∈𝒳{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathcal{X}

miny∈𝒴⁡p𝐟,𝐠​(y|𝐱)≥τ,miny∈𝒴⁡p𝐟′,𝐠′​(y|𝐱)≥τ.\displaystyle\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(y|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\geq\tau,\quad\min_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(y|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\geq\tau. (131)

Then

𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|^{2} ≤4​log⁡(τ)2τ​dKL​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′).\displaystyle\leq\frac{4\log(\tau)^{2}}{\tau}d_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}). (132)
Proof.

The result follows by integrating (126) using relation (9). ∎

Without assuming a lower bound on p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱)p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) we cannot derive a similar bound as 𝔼(KL(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅|𝐱)||p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱))2)\mathbb{E}(\mathrm{KL}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))^{2}) cannot be bounded even when KL(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅|𝐱)||p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱))\mathrm{KL}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})) is small.

Appendix F Bounding Representation Similarity in Terms of Canonical Correlations

We now investigate the implications for representation similarity. Recall that we consider two models specified by (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta with densities p𝐟,𝐠p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}} and p𝐟′,𝐠′p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}. Their representational dimensions are mm and m′m^{\prime} and in particular we do not assume that they agree. We denote by 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} and 𝐋′{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime} the matrices of unembeddings, that is

𝐋=(𝐠⁡(y1)…𝐠⁡(yk))∈ℝm×kand𝐋′=(𝐠′​(y1)⋯𝐠′​(yk))∈ℝm′×k.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{1})&\ldots&{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{k})\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}\quad\text{and}\quad{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}=\begin{pmatrix}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{1})&\cdots&{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{k})\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{\prime}\times k}. (142)

Note that the relations

𝐮⁡(𝐱)=𝐋⊤​𝐟​(𝐱),𝐮′​(𝐱)=𝐋′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),\quad{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) (143)

hold. We have seen in Theorem E.6 how to bound

∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2=∥𝐋⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐋′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)∥2\displaystyle\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}=\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2} (144)

in terms of the KL-divergence KL(p𝐟,𝐠(⋅|𝐱)||p𝐟′,𝐠′(⋅|𝐱))\mathrm{KL}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})||p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})). The goal of this section is to bound the canonical correlation coefficients between the random variables with samples (𝐠⁡(yi))1≤i≤k({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}))_{1\leq i\leq k} and (𝐠′​(yi))1≤i≤k({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i}))_{1\leq i\leq k} and the random variables 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime} by the expectation of the square logit difference. We denote by ρ1≥ρ2≥…≥ρmin⁡(m,m′)\rho_{1}\geq\rho_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\rho_{\min(m,m^{\prime})} the canonical correlations of 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} and 𝐠′{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime} which are given by the singular values of

(𝐋𝐋⊤)−1/2(𝐋𝐋′⁣⊤)(𝐋′𝐋′⁣⊤)−1/2.\displaystyle({\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\top})^{-1/2}({\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top})({\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top})^{-1/2}. (145)

Indeed, this holds because 𝐋𝐋⊤=k​Σ𝐠,𝐠∈ℝm×m{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\top}=k\Sigma_{{\bm{\mathrm{g}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}, 𝐋′​𝐋′⁣⊤=k​Σ𝐠′,𝐠′∈ℝm′×m′{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}=k\Sigma_{{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{\prime}\times m^{\prime}}, and 𝐋𝐋′⁣⊤=k​Σ𝐠,𝐠′∈ℝm×m′{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}=k\Sigma_{{\bm{\mathrm{g}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m^{\prime}}. Since the distribution p𝐟,𝐠p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}} is not invariant to embeddings shifts 𝐟+𝐜{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}+{\bm{\mathrm{c}}} it is natural to consider the moment-based canonical correlations of 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime} where instead of considering covariances one considers the second moments directly and we use the notation

𝐌𝐟,𝐟=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)​𝐟⊤​(𝐱)).\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}){\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\top}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})). (146)

We denote the moment-based canonical correlations of 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime} by ρ~1≥ρ~2≥…≥ρ~min⁡(m,m′)\tilde{\rho}_{1}\geq\tilde{\rho}_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\tilde{\rho}_{\min(m,m^{\prime})} which are given by the singular values of

𝐌𝐟,𝐟−1/2𝐌𝐟,𝐟′𝐌𝐟′,𝐟′−1/2.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}}^{-1/2}{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}}{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}}^{-1/2}. (147)

The result below extends to the standard canonical correlations with minor changes which we discuss in Appendix F.4.

To simplify the analysis slightly, we assume that 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} and 𝐋′{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime} have full rank mm and m′m^{\prime} and therefore, in particular, k≥max⁡(m,m′)+1k\geq\max(m,m^{\prime})+1 (the +1+1 arises because the unembeddings are centred and therefore linearly dependent (∑y∈𝒴𝐠⁡(y)=0\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)=0) so the rank can be at most k−1k-1). This implies that 𝐋𝐋⊤∈ℝm×m{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} and 𝐋′​𝐋′⁣⊤∈ℝm′×m′{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{\prime}\times m^{\prime}} are invertible matrices. Similarly we assume that the moment matrices 𝐌𝐟,𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}} and 𝐌𝐟′,𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}} defined in (146) have maximal rank mm and m′m^{\prime} respectively. Note that this follows from the diversity condition in Assumption 2.1 under minor regularity assumptions. We expect that extensions to the rank-deficient case are possible by considering the pseudoinverses (see Marconato et al. [2025] for a full discussion of the identifiability perspective in this case). Moreover, note that this assumption is not a real restriction because we could equivalently focus on the space generated by the vectors 𝐠⁡(yi){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}) and the projection of 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} on the orthogonal complement of this space is not identifiable anyway and similarly a degenerate 𝐌𝐟,𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}} results in arbitrary behaviour of 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} on the orthogonal complement of the column space of 𝐌𝐟,𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}}. Our upper bounds depend on diversity properties of one of the models (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) (typically the teacher model in a distillation setup) and it turns out that the right object to consider is the logit covariance

𝐌𝐮,𝐮=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​(𝐮⁡(𝐱)​𝐮⊤​(𝐱))=𝐋⊤​𝐌𝐟,𝐟​𝐋\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\top}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} (148)

which measures how spread out the logit distribution is. We remark that the logits are invariant to the model symmetries (𝐟,𝐠)→(𝐀𝐟,𝐀−⁣⊤​𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\to({\bm{\mathrm{A}}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{-\top}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}). Note that 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} and 𝐌𝐟,𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}} have maximal rank mm and so we denote the mm-nonzero eigenvalues of 𝐌𝐮,𝐮{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}} by μ1≥μ2≥…≥μm\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\mu_{m}. Note that small eigenvalues indicate that the representation does not exploit all dimensions of the embedding space and therefore this spectrum allows to quantify the diversity condition. After these preliminaries we can state the main result of this section.

Theorem F.1.

Consider two models (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}) and (𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) with representation dimensions mm and m′m^{\prime} and assume that 𝐌𝐟,𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}}, 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} and 𝐌𝐟′,𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}}, 𝐋′{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime} have maximal rank mm and m′m^{\prime} respectively. The canonical correlations ρi\rho_{i} (in decreasing order) of 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} and 𝐠′{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime} satisfy the bound

∑i=1m(1−ρi2)​μi≤𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}(1-\rho_{i}^{2})\mu_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2} (149)

where μi\mu_{i} are the eigenvalues of 𝐌𝐮,𝐮{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}} in decreasing order. Similarly the moment-based canonical correlations ρ~i\tilde{\rho}_{i} (in decreasing order) of 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime} satisfy

∑i=1m(1−ρ~i2)​μi≤𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}(1-\tilde{\rho}_{i}^{2})\mu_{i}\leq\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2} (150)

where we in both cases set ρi=ρ~i=0\rho_{i}=\tilde{\rho}_{i}=0 for i>m′i>m^{\prime} if m>m′m>m^{\prime}.

The goal of the next lemmas is to provide a proof of Theorem F.1, i.e., to show (149) and (150). The final summary of the proof can be found at the end of Appendix F.2. We note that the two bounds are essentially equivalent due to the symmetry of the problem in 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}, indeed note that the operation 𝐋𝐋⊤{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\top} just corresponds (up to a scalar) to building the covariance matrix from a random variables with finitely many values. Nevertheless, we show the two proofs separately below for the convenience of the reader. The general strategy of the proof is to regress 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} on 𝐋′{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime} and use this to decompose 𝐮​(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) (see Lemma F.2). Then one of the terms in the decomposition can be related to the canonical correlations ρi\rho_{i} (see Lemma F.4). Finally this relation can be used to bound the canonical correlation in Lemma F.5. We then extend the results to ρ~\tilde{\rho} using the same steps.

F.1 Bounding similarity of unembeddings

We consider the regression problem

𝐁=min𝐁¯∈ℝm×m′⁡∥𝐋−𝐁¯​𝐋′∥2.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}=\min_{\overline{{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m^{\prime}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}-\overline{{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}\rVert^{2}. (151)

The minimizer 𝐁{\bm{\mathrm{B}}} of this ordinary least squares problem is given by

𝐁=𝐋𝐋′⁣⊤​(𝐋′​𝐋′⁣⊤)−1.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}({\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top})^{-1}. (152)

We introduce the residual

𝚫=𝐋−𝐁𝐋′∈ℝm×k.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{\Delta}}}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}-{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}. (153)

We then find the following expansion.

Lemma F.2.

With the notation introduced above, in particular 𝐁=𝐋𝐋′⁣⊤​(𝐋′​𝐋′⁣⊤)−1{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}({\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top})^{-1} and 𝚫=𝐋−𝐁𝐋′{\bm{\mathrm{\Delta}}}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}-{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime} we can decompose

This lemma can be used to bound the norm of the residual ∥𝚫∥\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{\Delta}}}\rVert of the regression of 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} on 𝐠′{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}. Indeed, we find that

(155)

However, this bound is not invariant to model reparametrizations while the canonical correlations are. However, it is sufficient to conclude linear identifiability when the logits agree almost everywhere.

Proof of Theorem F.1.

Applying Lemma F.5 followed by Lemma F.2 we conclude that

which is (149). The bound (150) follows similarly from Lemma F.6 and F.9. ∎

F.3 Relating embeddings and unembeddings

The results in Theorem F.1 can be used to show that 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime} and 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} and 𝐠′{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime} are linearly related when the model logits are similar. Concretely we bounded the canonical correlations and we can also bound the residual (see Remark F.3). However, while these are quantitative versions of the linear identifiability of 𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}} and 𝐠{\bm{\mathrm{g}}} this alone is not sufficient to recover the identifiability result as this also requires that 𝐟=𝐁~​𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}=\tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}, 𝐠=𝐁𝐠′{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}={\bm{\mathrm{B}}}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime} and 𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤=𝐁~\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}=\tilde{\mathbf{B}}. Therefore, a natural question is whether we can show quantitative bounds for 𝐁⊤​𝐁~−𝟏m′×m′{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}-\bm{1}_{m^{\prime}\times m^{\prime}} (this matrix can also be considered for m′≠mm^{\prime}\neq m). However, when considering the equivalent model (𝐀⊤​𝐟′,𝐀−1​𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) for 𝐀∈GL⁡(m′){\bm{\mathrm{A}}}\in\mathrm{GL}(m^{\prime}) we find that the transition matrix becomes 𝐀−1​𝐁⊤​𝐁~​𝐀{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}. However, if 𝐁⊤​𝐁~{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}} is not a multiple of the identity we have

sup𝐀∈GL⁡(m′)∥𝐀−1​𝐁⊤​𝐁~​𝐀∥=∞\displaystyle\sup_{{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}\in\mathrm{GL}(m^{\prime})}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}\rVert=\infty (188)

and thus no meaningful bounds on ∥𝐁⊤​𝐁~∥\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}\rVert in terms of 𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2} are possible. Instead, we can only show a weaker statement for the relation of 𝐁{\bm{\mathrm{B}}} and 𝐁~\tilde{\mathbf{B}}. To achieve this we argue as in Lemmas F.2 and F.6.

Lemma F.10.

When 𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮′​(𝐱)−𝐮⁡(𝐱)∥2=0\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}=0, then 𝐁~⊤​𝐁~=𝟏m′×m′\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}=\bm{1}_{m^{\prime}\times m^{\prime}}. and the logits 𝐋′⁣⊤​𝐁⊤​𝐁~​𝐟′​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) of the model (𝐁𝐠′,𝐁~​𝐟′)({\bm{\mathrm{B}}}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime},\tilde{\mathbf{B}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}) also satisfy

(190)

One could derive bounds on ∥𝐁~⊤​𝐁~−𝟏m′×m′∥\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}-\bm{1}_{m^{\prime}\times m^{\prime}}\rVert when assuming lower bounds on the spectrum of the moments 𝐌𝐟′,𝐟′{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}} and 𝐋′​𝐋′⁣⊤{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}, however these assumptions are again not invariant under equivalence transformations of the model.

Proof.

We start from (174) and decompose the second term further using

Here the Pythagorean identity in the last step follows as in Lemma F.2 from 𝚫​𝐋′⁣⊤=0{\bm{\mathrm{\Delta}}}{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime\top}=0 (see (156)). From Lemma F.6 we infer that

F.4 Lower Bounds for the Mean Canonical Correlation

In this section we collect applications of Theorem F.1. The proof of Theorem 3.4 can be found at the end of this section. First we show how the theorem can be used to bound the mean canonical correlation coefficient, mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}.

Theorem F.12.

Assume the hypothesis of Theorem F.1, in particular we assume that the moment matrix 𝐌𝐮,𝐮=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​(𝐮⁡(𝐱)​𝐮​(𝐱)⊤){\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}){\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})^{\top}) has rank mm. Denote by μmin=μm>0\mu_{\min}=\mu_{m}>0 the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of 𝐌𝐮,𝐮{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}}. Then the bounds

∑i=1mρi≥∑i=1mρi2≥m−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2μminand\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\rho_{i}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\rho_{i}^{2}\geq m-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}}{\mu_{\min}}\quad\text{and} (194)
∑i=1mρ~i≥∑i=1mρ~i2≥m−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2μmin\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\rho}_{i}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\tilde{\rho}_{i}^{2}\geq m-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}}{\mu_{\min}} (195)

hold.

Proof.

Theorem F.1 implies

𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2μmin≥∑i=1m(1−ρi2)​μiμmin≥∑i=1m(1−ρi2)\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}}{\mu_{\min}}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}(1-\rho_{i}^{2})\frac{\mu_{i}}{\mu_{\min}}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}(1-\rho_{i}^{2}) (196)

where we used ρi2≤1\rho_{i}^{2}\leq 1 (so 1−ρi2≥01-\rho_{i}^{2}\geq 0) and μiμmin≥1\frac{\mu_{i}}{\mu_{\min}}\geq 1 in the last step. This implies the first bound and the second estimate follows similarly. ∎

Note that there are at most min⁡(m′,m)\min(m^{\prime},m) non-zero canonical correlations so the result directly implies lower bound on m′m^{\prime} to match the other models distribution. Or, stated equivalently, we can bound the information loss a smaller model must incur. In particular, we conclude lower bounds for the representation dimension of a student that tries to match the teacher’s logits with a given accuracy and those bounds are explicit functions of the teacher’s logits. This result can be slightly refined and we obtain the following theorem which closely resembles the reconstruction bound for PCA.

Theorem F.13.

Assume the hypothesis of Theorem F.1 and denote the eigenvalues of 𝐌𝐮,𝐮{\bm{\mathrm{M}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}} in decreasing order by μi\mu_{i}. Suppose the dimension m′m^{\prime} of the student model satisfies m′<mm^{\prime}<m. Then we find

𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2≥∑i=m′+1mμi.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}\geq\sum_{i=m^{\prime}+1}^{m}\mu_{i}. (197)
Proof.

The result follows from Theorem F.1 by using that ρi=0\rho_{i}=0 for i>m′i>m^{\prime}. ∎

Finally, we discuss the modifications to consider the standard covariance matrix based canonical correlations. For this, we will need the slightly stronger diversity condition that the covariance matrix

𝚺𝐮,𝐮=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​((𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​(𝐮⁡(𝐱)))​(𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​(𝐮⁡(𝐱)))⊤)\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{\Sigma}}}_{{\bm{\mathrm{u}}},{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\left(\left({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))\right)\left({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))\right)^{\top}\right) (198)

∑i=1mρi≥∑i=1mρi2≥m−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2μmand\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\rho_{i}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\rho_{i}^{2}\geq m-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}}{\mu_{m}}\quad\text{and} (199)
∑i=1mρ¯i≥∑i=1mρ¯i2≥m−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2μm\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bar{\rho}_{i}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bar{\rho}_{i}^{2}\geq m-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}}{\mu_{m}} (200)

hold.

Denote the mean of the embeddings by 𝐟¯=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​(𝐟​(𝐱))\bar{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})) and 𝐟¯′=𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​(𝐟′​(𝐱))\bar{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}}^{\prime}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})). where 𝐮{\bm{\mathrm{u}}} are the logits of the original model and a similar expression holds for 𝐮′{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}. ∑i=1mρ¯i≥∑i=1mρ¯i2≥m−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮c​(𝐱)−(𝐮′)c​(𝐱)∥2μm≥m−𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥2μm.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bar{\rho}_{i}\geq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bar{\rho}_{i}^{2}\geq m-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{c}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime})^{c}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}}{\mu_{m}}\geq m-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert^{2}}{\mu_{m}}. in the last step. The proof of (199) is similar. ∎

Appendix G Example of Models with small KL Divergence and Equal Embeddings, but Dissimilar Unembeddings

In this section, we illustrate why when we want to measure representational similarity that takes into account the equivalence relation of the identifiability class and why it is not enough to consider a measure on only similarity between the embeddings (or unembeddings).

We do this by constructing a pair of models with equal embeddings and small KL divergence, but dissimilar unembeddings as measured with mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}. Note that these models will also be dissimilar in terms of drepd_{\mathrm{rep}}, since drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} includes the unembeddings through the unembeddings matrices. These constructed models are displayed in Figs. 4 and 4

Assume we have models defining a distribution over 88 labels, i.e., 𝒴={y1,…,y8}\mathcal{Y}=\{y_{1},...,y_{8}\}, and with representation dimensionality m=2m=2. For a subset of input data, a reference model (𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta assigns high probability to one among the first four labels, as displayed by embeddings aligning to unembeddings directions 𝐠⁡(yi){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}), i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4. On the remaining input points, the model assign high mass, but equal probability, to either the labels y5y_{5} and y6y_{6}, or y7y_{7} and y8y_{8}. This can be seen from the embeddings aligned to 𝐠⁡(y5)+𝐠⁡(y6){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{5})+{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{6}) or to 𝐠⁡(y7)+𝐠⁡(y8){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{7})+{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{8}).

A second model (𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta has equal embeddings to (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}), that is 𝐟′​(𝐱)=𝐟​(𝐱){\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})={\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}) for all 𝐱∈𝒳{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\in\mathcal{X}, but dissimilar unembeddings. It is constructed so as to have equal unembeddings for the first 44 labels, i.e., 𝐠′​(yi)=𝐠⁡(yi){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{i})={\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i}) for i=1,…,4i=1,\ldots,4, and swapped unembeddings for y5y_{5} and y6y_{6} swapped and for y7y_{7} and y8y_{8}:

{𝐠′​(y5)=𝐠⁡(y6)𝐠′​(y6)=𝐠⁡(y5) and {𝐠′​(y7)=𝐠⁡(y8)𝐠′​(y8)=𝐠⁡(y7).\begin{cases}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{5})={\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{6})\\ {\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{6})={\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{5})\end{cases}\quad\text{ and }\quad\begin{cases}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{7})={\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{8})\\ {\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y_{8})={\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{7})\end{cases}\,. (204)

Despite the unembeddings of the models being dissimilar in a linear sense, we can now make dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}} arbitrarily small by increasing the norm of the embeddings or the unembeddings. Notice that the embeddings that are between the unembeddings on the left are exactly in the middle in terms of angle. Therefore, since all the unembeddings have the same norm, probability values of the two most likely labels will be equal for the two models. However, increasing the norm, will not make the unembeddings of the two models closer to being linear transformations of each other.

Note also that we can choose any of the first four labels y1,…,y4y_{1},...,y_{4}, to make the 𝐋,𝐋\mathbf{L},\mathbf{L} matrices with columns 𝐠~​(yi)\tilde{\mathbf{g}}(y_{i}), 𝐠~′​(yi)\tilde{\mathbf{g}}^{\prime}(y_{i}), and this will give us 𝐋=𝐋′\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{L^{\prime}}. In particular, we have 𝐀=𝐋−⁣⊤​𝐋′⊤=𝐈\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{L}^{-\top}\mathbf{L^{\prime}}^{\top}=\mathbf{I}, so

𝐟​(𝐱)=𝐀𝐟′​(𝐱)\displaystyle\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{f}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}) (205)

for all 𝐱\mathbf{x} like in the identifiability result, but we do not have the corresponding part for the unembeddings. That is, 𝐠~​(y)≠𝐀−⁣⊤​𝐠~′​(y)\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y)\neq{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{-\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y).

In terms of the mean canonical correlation, mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}, we have for the embeddings mCCA​(𝐟⁡(𝐱),𝐟′​(𝐱))=1m_{\mathrm{CCA}}({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}),{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))=1 and for the unembeddings mCCA​(𝐠⁡(y),𝐠′​(y))=0.67m_{\mathrm{CCA}}({\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y),{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}(y))=0.67 (The mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}} for the unembeddings can be made smaller by spreading out unembeddings for labels y5,y6,y7,y8y_{5},y_{6},y_{7},y_{8} further).

Thus, we see that there can be a perfect linear relationship between embeddings and, even if the distributions are very close in terms of KL divergence, there is still no guarantee for the unembeddings to be similar up to the inverse linear transformation of the embeddings.

Appendix H Theoretical Material for Section 3.4: The Logit Distance Bounds the Linear Identifiability Dissimilarity

In this section, we will first show how the squared distance between logits can be written as a normalized distance between representations Section H.1, and then show how the logit distance bounds the linear identifiability dissimilarity from Definition 3.7 in Section H.2.

H.1 Connection Between Distance between Logits and Representations

Theorem H.1.

Let p,p′p,p^{\prime} be as defined above, and mm the dimension of the representations. Let N=(k−2m−1)N=\binom{k-2}{m-1}. Then the squared distance between logits can be written as a normalized distance between the representations in the following sense: Let 𝐋~𝒥=𝐔𝐃𝐕⊤\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}={\bm{\mathrm{U}}}{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top} be the singular value decomposition of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, and let 𝐁~𝒥=𝐃−1​𝐔⊤\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}={\bm{\mathrm{D}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}. Then we have

‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖22=12​k​N​∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖22.\displaystyle\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2kN}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\left\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\;. (206)
Proof.

We consider the norm on the right hand side of Eq. 206:

‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖22\displaystyle\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}^{2} (207)
=∥𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤𝐋~𝒥−⁣⊤(𝐋~𝒥⊤𝐟(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⊤𝐟′(𝐱))∥22\displaystyle=\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left(\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}^{2} (208)
=∥(𝐁~𝒥𝐋~𝒥)−⁣⊤(𝐋~𝒥⊤𝐟(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⊤𝐟′(𝐱))∥22\displaystyle=\|(\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}})^{-\top}\left(\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}^{2} (209)

Using the definition of 𝐁~𝒥=𝐃−1​𝐔⊤\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}={\bm{\mathrm{D}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top} and recalling that the singular value decomposition of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} was 𝐋~𝒥=𝐔𝐃𝐕⊤\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}={\bm{\mathrm{U}}}{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}, we see that

𝐁~𝒥​𝐋~𝒥=𝐃−1​𝐔⊤​𝐔𝐃𝐕⊤=𝐕⊤\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}={\bm{\mathrm{D}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}={\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top} (210)

So we have that

∥(𝐁~𝒥𝐋~𝒥)−⁣⊤(𝐋~𝒥⊤𝐟(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⊤𝐟′(𝐱))∥22\displaystyle\|(\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}})^{-\top}\left(\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}^{2} (211)
=∥𝐕⊤(𝐋~𝒥⊤𝐟(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⊤𝐟′(𝐱))∥22\displaystyle=\|{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}\left(\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}^{2} (212)

Now since 𝐕⊤{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top} is an orthonormal matrix, it does not change the norm of a vector. Recall, that for a vector 𝐚{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}, we have:

‖𝐕⊤​𝐚‖22=(𝐕⊤​𝐚)⊤​𝐕⊤​𝐚=𝐚⊤​𝐕𝐕⊤​𝐚=𝐚⊤​𝐚=‖𝐚‖22\displaystyle\|{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\|_{2}^{2}=({\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{a}}})^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}={\bm{\mathrm{a}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}={\bm{\mathrm{a}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}=\|{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\|_{2}^{2} (213)

So we have that

∥𝐕⊤(𝐋~𝒥⊤𝐟(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⊤𝐟′(𝐱))∥22\displaystyle\|{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top}\left(\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}^{2} (214)
=∥𝐋~𝒥⊤𝐟(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⊤𝐟′(𝐱)∥22\displaystyle=\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2} (215)

So using Lemma D.4, we see that

12​k​N​∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖22\displaystyle\frac{1}{2kN}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}^{2} =12​k​N∑y~∈𝒴∑𝒥⊆𝒴∖{y~}𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱∥𝐋~𝒥⊤𝐟(𝐱)−𝐋~𝒥′⊤𝐟′(𝐱)∥22\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2kN}\sum_{\tilde{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\setminus\{\tilde{y}\}}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{{}^{\prime}\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2}^{2} (216)
=‖𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)‖22\displaystyle=\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2}^{2} (217)

∎

This gives us the following corollary (Corollary 3.8 from the main paper):

Corollary H.2.

For (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta, we have

drep​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))=0⇔dlogit​(p𝐟,𝐠,p𝐟′,𝐠′)=0.\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{rep}}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))=0\iff d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}},p_{{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}})=0\,.
Proof.

“⟸\impliedby”: Assume dlogit​(p,p′)=0d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime})=0. Since dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}} is a metric between probability distributions, this gives us p=p′p=p^{\prime}. Therefore, Corollary 3.6 gives us drep​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))=0d_{\mathrm{rep}}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))=0.

“⟹\implies”: Assume drep​((𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟′,𝐠′))=0d_{\mathrm{rep}}(({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}))=0. From Theorem H.1 we get that dlogit​(p,p′)=0d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime})=0. ∎

H.2 Logit Distance Bounds the Linear Identifiability Dissimilarity

In this section we present the full proof of Theorem 3.9, however, we first prove a lemma to help with the main result.

Lemma H.3.

Let (𝐟,𝐠),(𝐟,𝐠)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}),({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}})\in\Theta. Let 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} be as defined in the priliminaries Eq. 4, and let 𝐋~𝒥=𝐔𝐃𝐕⊤\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}={\bm{\mathrm{U}}}{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}{\bm{\mathrm{V}}}^{\top} be the singular value decomposition of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}. Let 𝐁~𝒥=𝐃−1​𝐔⊤\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}={\bm{\mathrm{D}}}^{-1}{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}. Let σ𝐋~𝒥​min\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min} be the smallest singular value of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, and let σmin\sigma_{\min} be the smallest singular value of all 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}. Then for every choice of labels and input, 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}, we have the following bounds:

‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2σmin≥‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2σ𝐋~𝒥​min≥‖𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\frac{\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}}{\sigma_{\min}}\geq\frac{\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}}{\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}}\geq\|{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2} (218)

And similarly, if we let σ𝐋~𝒥​max\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\max} be the largest singular value of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, and σmax\sigma_{\max} be the largest singular value of all 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, we also have:

‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2σmax≤‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2σ𝐋~𝒥​max≤‖𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\frac{\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}}{\sigma_{\max}}\leq\frac{\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}}{\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\max}}\leq\|{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\|_{2} (219)
Proof.

We consider the norm on the left hand side of Eq. 218:, where we recall that 𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤=𝐃𝐔⊤\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}={\bm{\mathrm{D}}}{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}:

‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2\displaystyle\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2} (220)
=‖𝐃𝐔⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2\displaystyle=\|{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2} (221)
=‖𝐃⁡(𝐔⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐔⊤​𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2\displaystyle=\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}\left({\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right\|_{2} (222)

Now 𝐃{\bm{\mathrm{D}}} is the diagonal matrix with the singular values of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} in the diagonal. We define 𝐃min{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}_{\min} to be the diagonal matrix with the minimum singular value of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, σ𝐋~𝒥​min\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}, in all the diagonal entries. This means that multiplying a vector with 𝐃min{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}_{\min} will make the norm smaller compared to multiplying with 𝐃{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}. In other words, we have:

‖𝐃⁡(𝐔⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐔⊤​𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2≥‖𝐃min​(𝐔⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐔⊤​𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2\displaystyle\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}\left({\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right\|_{2}\geq\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}_{\min}\left({\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right\|_{2} (223)

We can calculate the effect of multiplying a vector, 𝐚{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}, with 𝐃min{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}_{\min}:

‖𝐃min​𝐚‖2=∑i=1D(σ𝐋~𝒥​min​ai)2=σ𝐋~𝒥​min2​∑i=1Dai2=σ𝐋~𝒥​min​∑i=1Dai2=σ𝐋~𝒥​min​‖𝐚‖2\displaystyle\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}_{\min}{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\right\|_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{D}(\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}a_{i})^{2}}=\sqrt{\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{D}a_{i}^{2}}=\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{D}a_{i}^{2}}=\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{a}}}\right\|_{2} (224)

So we have that

‖𝐃min​(𝐔⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐔⊤​𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2\displaystyle\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}_{\min}\left({\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right\|_{2} (225)
=σ𝐋~𝒥​min​‖𝐔⊤​𝐟​(𝐱)−𝐔⊤​𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle=\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2} (226)
=σ𝐋~𝒥​min​‖𝐔⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2\displaystyle=\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right\|_{2} (227)

Since 𝐔⊤{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top} is an orthonormal matrix, it does not change the norm of a vector, so we have that

σ𝐋~𝒥​min​‖𝐔⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2\displaystyle\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{U}}}^{\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\right\|_{2} (228)
=σ𝐋~𝒥​min​‖𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle=\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2} (229)

All in all, we have that for any choice of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}} and 𝐱{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}:

‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2≥σ𝐋~𝒥​min​‖𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}\geq\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2} (230)

which means that

‖𝐁~𝒥−⁣⊤​(𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱))‖2σ𝐋~𝒥​min≥‖𝐟⁡(𝐱)−𝐀~𝒥​𝐟′​(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\frac{\|\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{B}}}_{\mathcal{J}}^{-\top}\left({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right)\|_{2}}{\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min}}\geq\left\|{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}_{\mathcal{J}}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\right\|_{2} (231)

And since σmin≤σ𝐋~𝒥​min\sigma_{\min}\leq\sigma_{\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}\min} we get the second inequality.

We can make a similar argument by defining 𝐃max{\bm{\mathrm{D}}}_{\max} as the diagonal matrix with the maximum singular value of 𝐋~𝒥\tilde{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}_{\mathcal{J}}, σ𝐋​max\sigma_{{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}\max}, in all the diagonal entries, and go through the steps from Eq. 223 with the inequality reversed.

∎

We are now ready to prove the main result:

Theorem H.4.

Let p,p′p,p^{\prime} be as before, and mm the dimension of the representations and kk the number of labels. Let C=2​mk−1C=\sqrt{\frac{2m}{k-1}}. Appendix I Proof of Theorem 4.3

In this Section we show that when dlogit​(p,p′)d_{\mathrm{logit}}(p,p^{\prime}) between two models is small, then concepts in one model are approximately represented in another model, in particular we prove Theorem 4.3. We recall that 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} is the matrix of unembeddings and that a concept 𝐡{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} defines a conditional distribution p𝐡​(c∣𝐱)p_{\bm{\mathrm{h}}}(c\mid{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}), over C≥2C\geq 2 values.

Consider a model (𝐟,𝐠)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}), such that 𝐡{\bm{\mathrm{h}}} is linearly represented in𝐟{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}. For every c∈{1,…,C}c\in\{1,\ldots,C\}, we write the concept vectors 𝐰c∈ℝm{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} as 𝐋​𝜶c{\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{\alpha}}}_{c} for some 𝜶c∈ℝk{\bm{\mathrm{\alpha}}}_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} which we call concept weights as they are the weights when writing 𝐰c=∑i=1k𝐠⁡(yi)​(αc)i{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{c}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y_{i})(\alpha_{c})_{i}. Since we assume that 𝐋{\bm{\mathrm{L}}} has full rank, this is possible for all 𝐰c{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{c}. Moreover, this is a natural way to parametrize the concepts as it is invariant to linear transformations of the embedding space and concepts of interest are generally aligned with the unembeddings 𝐠⁡(y){\bm{\mathrm{g}}}(y). We also define the matrix 𝐀=(𝜶c)c∈{1,…,C}∈ℝk×C{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}=({\bm{\mathrm{\alpha}}}_{c})_{c\in\{1,\ldots,C\}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times C} and this is related to the concept weight matrix through 𝐖=𝐋𝐀{\bm{\mathrm{W}}}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}.

We now show that these concepts can be approximately realized on the embedding space of another model (𝐟′,𝐠′)∈Θ({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime})\in\Theta when the logit distance to (𝐟′,𝐠′)({\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime},{\bm{\mathrm{g}}}^{\prime}) is small. Indeed, we consider the concept matrix

𝐖′=𝐋′​𝐀′∈ℝm×C\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{W}}}^{\prime}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{A}}}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times C} (246)

and therefore the individual concept vectors are given by

𝐰c′=𝐋′​𝜶c′.\displaystyle{\bm{\mathrm{w}}}^{\prime}_{c}={\bm{\mathrm{L}}}^{\prime}{\bm{\mathrm{\alpha}}}^{\prime}_{c}. (247)

We can then define (the biases remain invariant bc=bc′b_{c}=b_{c}^{\prime})

p𝐡′​(c|𝐱)=exp⁡(𝐰c′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)+bc)∑j=1Cexp⁡(𝐰j′⁣⊤​𝐟′​(𝐱)+𝐛j)\displaystyle p^{\prime}_{{\bm{\mathrm{h}}}}(c|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})=\frac{\exp\big({\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{c}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})+b_{c}\big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{C}\exp\big({\bm{\mathrm{w}}}_{j}^{\prime\top}{\bm{\mathrm{f}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})+{\bm{\mathrm{b}}}_{j}\big)} (248)

Appendix J L1L_{1} Based Loss Bounds Distribution Distance

We here present the proof of the following statement:

Proposition J.1.

Assume that pp, p′p^{\prime} are two models which both satisfy Assumption 3.2 for some τ>0\tau>0. Then

𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥22≤2​|log⁡(τ)|​𝔼𝐱∼p𝐱​∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥1.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2|\log(\tau)|\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}\sim p_{{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}}}\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert_{1}. (258)
Proof.

Note that 1≥p⁡(y|𝐱)≥τ1\geq p(y|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\geq\tau and thus 0≥log⁡(p⁡(y|𝐱))≥log⁡(τ)0\geq\log(p(y|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))\geq\log(\tau) which also implies 0≥log(p(⋅|𝐱))¯≥log⁡(τ)0\geq\overline{\log(p(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}\geq\log(\tau) denoting again by ⋅¯\overline{\cdot} the average over the labels. Then we can apply (129) and get

(𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱))i2=|log⁡(p⁡(yi|𝐱))−log(p(⋅|𝐱))¯−log⁡(p′​(yi|𝐱))+log(p′(⋅|𝐱))¯|⋅|(𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱))i|≤2​|log⁡(τ)|⋅|(𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱))i|.\displaystyle\begin{split}({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))_{i}^{2}&=\left|\log(p(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))-\overline{\log(p(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}-\log(p^{\prime}(y_{i}|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))+\overline{\log(p^{\prime}(\cdot|{\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))}\right|\cdot|({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))_{i}|\\ &\leq 2|\log(\tau)|\cdot|({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))_{i}|.\end{split} (259)

We conclude that

∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥22≤2​|log⁡(τ)|⋅∑i=1k|(𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱))i|=2​|log⁡(τ)|⋅∥𝐮⁡(𝐱)−𝐮′​(𝐱)∥1.\displaystyle\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2|\log(\tau)|\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{k}|({\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}}))_{i}|=2|\log(\tau)|\cdot\lVert{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})-{\bm{\mathrm{u}}}^{\prime}({\bm{\mathrm{x}}})\rVert_{1}. Appendix K Additional Details on Experiments

Our code is available at https://github.com/bemigini/logit-distance-bounds-rep-sim.

Synth

consists of 77 classes distributed over 44 spiral rays. The dataset is created to ensure that, in input space, there are not two classes that are always close to each other and that input data are not linearly separable.

We generate 2​d2d input data as follows: for each of the seven classes, we define four angles, each capturing the starting angle of one of the spirals. Then, for each of these rays with angle θ0\theta_{0}, varying the radius ρ∈[1,10]\rho\in[1,10], we randomly sample a point near the spirals with an angle

θi=θ0+2​π/T⋅ρ/10+ϵ\theta_{i}=\theta_{0}+2\pi/T\cdot\rho/10+\epsilon (261)

where TT denotes the period of the spiral and ϵ∼Unif⁡(−σ⁡(ρ),σ⁡(ρ))\epsilon\sim\mathrm{Unif}(-\sigma(\rho),\sigma(\rho)) is sampled so to ensure that it never crosses other spiral rays, by regulating the interval [−σ⁡(ρ),σ⁡(ρ)][-\sigma(\rho),\sigma(\rho)] on the value of ρ\rho. The dataset is visualized in Fig. 2.

Training data amount to 1414k instances, while the validation and test dataset each comprise 77k data points.

CIFAR.

We use the CIFAR100 [Krizhevsky et al., 2009] loaded from torchvision with the original split with 500 images per class for training and 100 images per class for testing. So all in all 50,000 images for training and 10,000 images for test. We do not make a validation split for this dataset.

SUB

is a regenerated version of CUB200 [Wah et al., 2011], a dataset for bird classification with annotation on salient bird features. In SUB, data points are annotated with a label YY capturing the bird specie, and a concept CC indicating the attribute which was modified during generation.

The dataset contains a total of 38.438.4k images, splitted in 21.521.5k for training, 5.35.3k for validation, and 11.511.5k for test. It comprises 3333 annotated class labels. Each image is also annotated with a concept reflecting a salient feature of the bird that has been modified during generation, such as the color of the breast or the shape of the beak, for a total of 3333 different concept attributes.

We use both these annotations to train teacher models. This enforces the teacher to both linearly encode concepts and labels in the embeddings.

K.1 Architectures and hyperparameters details

For Synth, we adopt an MLP constituted of 22 hidden layers, each with 512512 units and ReLU activations. Teachers and students use this architecture and map to a (m=2)(m=2) representation space.

Teachers are trained for 15001500 epochs, while students are trained for 250250 epochs on the training set annotated with teacher’s probabilities. For all runs, we use a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} with exponential decay on each epoch set to γ=0.995\gamma=0.995, and batch size of 512512.

For CIFAR 100100, we use ResNet[He et al., 2016] models for the embedding part of both teacher and student, but of different sizes. For the teacher, we use a ResNet50 and for the student a ResNet18 with the same architecture as implemented by torchvision55 5 docs.pytorch.org/vision/main/models/generated/torchvision.models.resnet50.html. The final linear layer of the embedding model for both student and teacher goes to 5050 dimensions. For the unembeddings we use a single linear layer, giving us 100100 (one for each label) 5050-dimensional unembeddings. We initialize the teacher model with weights trained on ImageNet taken from torchvision (ResNet50_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V2) and train the teacher for 10 epochs on the train split of the CIFAR dataset. Each student is then trained for 50 epochs on the training set with either ℒlogit1\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{logit}}^{1} (L1L_{1} student), dlogit2d_{\mathrm{logit}}^{2} (L2L_{2} student), or KL divergence (KL student) between student and teacher distributions as a loss. For all runs on CIFAR, we use a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} with exponential decay on each epoch set to γ=0.995\gamma=0.995, and batch size of 3232.

For SUB, we first preprocess all images with DINOv2 [Oquab et al., 2023], mapping them to 768768 dimensional embeddings. Then, we train a shallow neural network with 10241024 units, with ReLU activations, dropout set to p=0.1p=0.1 and BatchNorm. Both teachers and students have the same architecture, and the representations for all models are (m=10)(m=10)-dimensional.

Teachers and students are trained for 500500 epochs to ensure convergence and, for all runs, we use a learning rate of 5⋅10−35\cdot 10^{-3} with exponential decay on each epoch set to γ=0.995\gamma=0.995, and batch size of 512512.

K.2 Metrics Evaluation

We use sklearn.evaluation for label and concept accuracy, while we implement with torch the evaluation of dKLd_{\mathrm{KL}}, dlogitd_{\mathrm{logit}}, and use sklearn.cross_decomposition.CCA to evaluate mCCAm_{\mathrm{CCA}}.

To evaluate drepd_{\mathrm{rep}}, we adopt the following procedure. Depending on the number of labels, evaluating all possible choices of pivots and subsets of labels can be unfeasible. We thus consider selecting at random the pivots and the subset of labels to reduce the computational cost. For Synth, we evaluate drepd_{\mathrm{rep}} for all possible labels and pivots. For CIFAR we select all possible pivots and for each of them we consider 200200 subsets of labels selected at random among the

(100−150)≈5⋅1028\binom{100-1}{50}\approx 5\cdot 10^{28}

possible combinations. For SUB, we select all possible pivots and for each of them we consider 250250 subsets of labels selected at random among the

(33−110)≈6⋅107\binom{33-1}{10}\approx 6\cdot 10^{7}

possible combinations. This number of samples is very small compared to the total number of combinations possible, but the most important thing is that we get information from all possible labels and with 200200(250250) samples of 5050(1010) labels, we can be relatively sure to draw each of the 100100(3333) labels at least once.

Aggregation of measures. Reported values on teachers are aggregating by evaluating the mean and standard deviations over 55 runs. For each teacher, we run 55 different seeds for both the KL\mathrm{KL} student and the L1L_{1} student, and evaluate the mean value μi\mu_{i} and variance σi2\sigma_{i}^{2}, for i∈{1,…,5}i\in\{1,\ldots,5\}. We then aggregate all mean and variances by considering the inverse-variance weighting. The mean is given by

ωi=1σi2,μ¯=∑ωi​μi∑iωi,\omega_{i}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}},\quad\bar{\mu}=\frac{\sum\omega_{i}\mu_{i}}{\sum_{i}\omega_{i}}\,, (262)

whereas the standard deviation is obtained as

σ¯=1∑iωi.\bar{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\sum_{i}\omega_{i}}}\,. (263)

The final results are reported as μ¯±σ¯\bar{\mu}\pm\bar{\sigma} for all metrics.

K.3 Extended results

We report here the full result of our experimental investigation on the three dataset we consider. Precision is set to 33 for all tables and metrics.
